Not only are they considered one of the most antioxidant-rich fruits, with nearly 33 times the antioxidant content than black grapes, but they also contain 16 amino acids, are an excellent source of minerals such as potassium, calcium, zinc, magnesium, and iron, and are rich in vitamins E and C. Our 100% pure frozen pulp is just as delicious as the fruit itself! And with no added colours, preservatives, or flavourings added, you can feel confident knowing that the pulp is nutritionally beneficial. NAME: Achacha
Description:
The achacha is a highly prized tropical fruit. With its sweet, tangy, refreshing taste it adds a new flavour to the fruit bowl! The achachas firm orange skin peels away easily to reveal a subtly sweet-then-tart white interior. The fruits can contain one or two large seeds. Achachas originated in the Bolivian Amazon Rainforest, and are now cultivated largely in Australia.
Achachas are a valuable source of vitamin C and folate, as well as potassium, riboflavin and antioxidants. The sugar levels of the achacha are relatively low compared to other fruits.

NAME: African cherry (agbalumo)
Description:
The African cherry, mainly cultivated in West Africa, is an underrated fruit that dazzles people's tastebuds with its unique array of flavours - the skin, flesh, and seeds all have a different taste, making for an unforgettable eating experience!
Also known as African star apples, so-called because inside each fruit is a cluster of large seeds stuck together in the shape of a star, these tangerine-sized fruits have tough, almost leather-like skin, which changes from green to dark orange in colour as it ripens. When ripe, the fruits have tender, fibrous dark red/orange flesh that offers eaters a delightful flavour combination, intriguingly containing notes of both sweetness and tartness, with subtle acidic, citrus hints.
Embedded within the flesh are seeds with shiny brown casings (which feel like plastic), covered with a cream-ish white, fibrous, sweet membrane.
Not only are African cherries incredibly delicious, but they are also extremely nutritious: they are an excellent source of calcium and fibre, are rich in iron, and also contain good amounts of vitamins A and C, boasting higher levels of vitamin C than oranges!
Although most commonly eaten fresh out of hand, African cherries can be used in food and drink recipes too, from smoothies and mocktails to desserts! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourites, including an amazing African cherry ice cream!
Don't forget our frozen African cherries too. They are a real treat to be enjoyed when the fresh fruit is out of season.

Indeed, navigating an alkaline diet can be difficult because even fruits that we consider acidic still have an alkaline effect on the body. For example, lemons and limes have a rather acidic pH, yet they actually have an alkalizing effect on the body. This is why we've made this bespoke selection box - you can buy this knowing you'll receive truly alkaline fruits and vegetables.
Alkaline diets have become very popular in recent years, gaining celebrity followers such as Victoria Beckham, Jennifer Aniston, and Gwyneth Paltrow, because eating alkaline foods is considered vital for maintaining pH balance in the body - in other words, it is believed that alkaline fruits can effectively neutralize the very high acid levels (scored at 2 on the pH scale) in the stomach.

NAME: Aloe vera leaf and plant
Description:
Aloe vera, a succulent plant species originating from the Arabian Peninsula - it grows wild in tropical, semi-tropical, and arid climates around the world - is globally renowned for its medicinal and cosmetic uses. Indeed, thanks to the multitude of beneficial ways it can be put to use, particularly its health and skin care benefits, aloe vera is often described as the 'wonder plant'!
The aloe vera leaf is green and firm on the outside, creating a shield from its soft jelly-like flesh. Both the skin and the gel inside aloe vera leaves can be eaten, but make sure to wash the skin or gel thoroughly before consumption to remove all traces of latex, which can have unpleasant and potentially harmful side effects.
It has become popular to mix aloe vera flesh with a variety of different ingredients to make refreshing, invigorating juices and smoothies - check out the 'Further information' tab below for our recommended recipes! As aloe vera is rich in many antioxidants, has anti-inflammatory properties, and may aid digestion, you can be happy knowing that these drinks are nutritionally beneficial as well as rejuvenating. Caution: Aloin, present in the outer layer (green skin) is toxic. Remove the outer layer (green skin) and rinse the flesh before use. Not recommended for pregnant and lactating women and children under 12 years.

NAME: Amla
Description:
Amla, also known as Indian gooseberry, are small, round - they are roughly the size of a marble - berries perfect for a variety of culinary uses!
Native to the subtropical South Asian countries of India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh, these berries have tough, yet thin, light-green skin, and flesh that is crisp and juicy, and contains an interesting hexagonal-shaped stone with 6 small seeds. The taste of the flesh is intriguing: it has a mix of flavours unlike any other fruits we've tried, ranging in one bite from a rich earthiness to a sour bitterness.
The grape-like berries can be eaten fresh, though the bitter taste is better offset with a sprinkle of salt, so traditionally they're used for making delicious pickles and chutneys. However, their unique, multi-dimensional flavour means they are ideal for use in a variety of recipes, suiting both sweet and savoury applications. We'd recommend using these fruits to make amla murabba, a delightful sweet preserve served with Indian flatbread, bake them into tarts and other sweet treats, or juice them to create delectable flavourings for vinegars and marinades. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipes!
As well as being extremely versatile, amla are also believed to have excellent nutritional value, and indeed are highly revered in Ayurvedic medicine. In particular, they are rich in vitamin C and many antioxidants, and are regarded as being beneficial in supporting healthy digestion.

NAME: Apple - butter fuji
Description:
Butter Fuji apples are one of the most attractive modern apple varieties!
Also known as golden Fuji or cream fuji apples due to their glossy pale yellow skin, these eye-catching fruits from China are the same variety as Fuji apples, but have been covered in bags while growing so their peel gains this distinctively soft colouring instead of the red of their more well-known counterpart.
Round in shape and around 3 inches in diameter, butter Fuji apples have smooth, delicate skin and flesh that is firm, yet softer than conventional apple varieties and wonderfully succulent. Like regular Fujis, they contain between 9-11% sugars by weight and have a dense flesh that is sweeter and lighter than many other apple cultivars, making them popular with consumers around the world. Indeed, many people think butter Fujis have an even more delicious taste than the red variety - the fact that they stay on their trees for at least a month longer than red Fujis, butter Fujis are commonly praised for boasting an even sweeter flavour, with especially pronounced notes of honey.
Although best enjoyed simply eaten fresh out of hand, cream Fujis are also perfect for adding some colour to your fruit and green salads - they combine particularly well with walnuts, almonds, cranberries, and pears - and are well suited to pairing with cheeses such as cheddar. You can also use Fuji apples in any recipe that calls for apples - check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our recommended recipes, including one for a quick and easy apple crisp, the perfect dessert!
As well as being delicious, cream Fujis are packed full of beneficial nutrients. As well as a high sugar content, they are an excellent source of fibre and are rich in vitamin C and omega-3.
Fuji apples are an apple hybrid developed by growers at Tohoku Research Station in Fujisaki, Aomori, Japan in the late 1930s. It originated as a cross between two American apple varieties - the Red Delicious and old Virginia Ralls Genet apples.

NAME: Apple - meigetsu (luxury fruit for gifting)
Description:
Japanese apples arent like just any other apple, they are rare treats!
Meaning beautiful moon in Japanese, Meigetsu apples are a premium variety from the gunma prefecture in Japan traditionally given as gifts to friends and family or anyone who appreciated perfect fruit.
Beneath firm, matte, yellow-green skin is a crisp, fine-grained flesh bursting with sweetness. In fact, they are so renowned for their honey-like sweetness, juiciness and low acidity that, in Japan, they are viewed more as a candy-like treat or dessert than a fruit! Their sugar content is 15, which is almost the same as mangoes and the famous Yubari king melon.
Due to the high level of dedication and expertise require to grow Meigetsu apples, their low yield makes them extremely rare. This, paired with their popularity means that they are often sold out in harvest time every year and are rarely seen in the market. This could be your chance to one of the sweetest apples in the world, for yourself!

NAME: Apple - red flesh 'redlove', 'kissabel' and 'rosetta'
Description:
Are you a lover of apples? Well, red flesh apples will be just the thing for you!
We source two varieties of red flesh apples: kissabel and redlove.
Our kissabel apples, grown in England, have aesthetically pleasing golden yellow/orange skin, with a slight red blush that matches the appealing rosy-coloured flesh. One bite of these fruits and you will fall in love: your tastebuds will be in heaven when you bite into the crisp, crunchy, sweet flesh, especially when you experience the wonderfully tangy aftertaste! Many people describe the flavour as being comparable to a mix of apple and pear.
Redlove apples are similarly brilliant. These hybrid fruits developed in Switzerland are red both on the outside and inside, making these glossy, smooth apples a real treat for the eyes. They have a strong, fruity-sweet aroma and, like kissabel apples, their flesh is firm, crunchy, and superbly succulent. Redlove apples are slightly less tart than kissabel apples, with their tartness offset by sweet undertones and tangy notes similar to cherries and berries.
Rosetta apples, grown in England, are a rare early season variety that get their name for the rosette pattern that emerges when you cut them open. Beneath their thick smooth skin is a pink marbled flesh that has a light delicate sweet flavour with notes of berry. As a dessert apple, they are best consumed straight out of hand.
Delectable when eaten out of hand as a regular apple, they are also perfect for brightening up and adding some crispness to fruit salads - especially because the highly oxidized flesh doesn't turn brown when sliced, unlike regular apples! - making apple juice or cider, and are well-suited to baking applications. Indeed, redlove apples are particularly valued not only for their bright red hue but due to the fact that they are equally capable of being used as an eating and a cooking apple. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some fantastic recipes!
Additionally, red flesh apples boast numerous health benefits. As well as being full of antioxidants - redlove apples have an antioxidant content that is 30-40% higher than regular apples! - they are rich in anthocyanins, which can help protect the immune system, and are an excellent source of fibre, potassium, and vitamins A and C.

NAME: Apple - sun fuji (luxury fruit for gifting)
Description:
Discover the exquisite sun fuji apple from Aomori Prefecture in Japan. The perfect luxury fruit for gifting to an apple or fruit connoisseur. For someone who appreciates the finest food.
Renowned for its vibrant red skin that mirrors the sun, this apple not only captivates the eye but also boasts a unique 'honey core.' This natural feature is the sugars in the apples moving to the centre to provide a remarkable defense against the extreme temperature fluctuations typical of the Fuji Mountain region. The apples can be exposed to temperatures between -20 to +10 in the same day! Apples from trees with the most prominent honey-core attract the highest market rate. Please note though, once the sun fuji apples are exposed to stable warmer temperatures the honey core gradually dicipates as the sugars evenly distributes across the whole flesh. It's for this reason that we can't guarantee your sun fuji will have the honey core characteristic.
Each bite reveals a rich flavour, an elevated apple experience.
Its delightful sweetness and hint of acidity make the sun fuji apple a cherished treat in Japan, and increasingly more here at one as luxury fruit is being discovered in the UK.
For a special occasion, or as an elegant addition to any gift basket. Indulge yourself, or someone special, with this exceptional fruit.

Although small in size - they are only 1-3cm in diameter! - arbutus are a delightful fruit that deserve much more attention!
Arbutus, also known as strawberry tree fruits, are red berries which are first and foremost visually distinctive, their spiky red surface dazzling the eye. After the 12 months they take to mature, becoming fully ripe typically in autumn, the golden flesh of these wonderful fruits emits a fragrant aroma, similar to that of anise, and has a refreshing, sweet taste, with a flavour reminiscent of an intriguing combination of fig, peach and kousa dogwod.
They are edible fresh, but are usually found preserved in tins or dried, especially because the mature fruit tends to bruise very easily, making transportation difficult - our frozen and canned arbutus are therefore the perfect way to enjoy these fruits!
Arbutus are most commonly used mostly for making jams, marmalades, jellies, sauces and yoghurts and even alcoholic beverages, such as the Portuguese medronho, a type of strong brandy! Many regions of Albania also prepare the traditional drink rakia from the arbutus fruit. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recommended recipes.
As well as being versatile in their uses, arbutus also boast nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of antioxidant vitamins such as vitamin C, beta-carotene, and niacin.

NAME: Avocado - Caribbean or Ugandan
Description:
We sell two varieties of avocado - Caribbean and Ugandan - that, though slightly different, both taste divine!
If we had to pick a favourite, though, it would be Caribbean avocadoes. These avocadoes are generally considered to well surpass other types in terms of quality and taste, primarily because they are harvested when fully mature and then sent to the UK by air, unlike other varieties which are harvested early and held in refrigeration for extended periods whilst sent to the UK by sea.
Our Caribbean avocados grow abundantly on the tropical islands of St Lucia and Jamaica. They are round, plump and usually of medium to large size, with a fairly large round seed in the centre. They're harvested when glossy green but ripen to maroon red and eventually deep purple.
With a heavenly, melt-in-the-mouth texture, being supremely creamy and buttery, and a flavour that dazzles the tastebuds with its delightful sweetness, it's no wonder they are so adored by the locals! Make sure you leave them to ripen perfectly before eating so you enjoy the flesh at its finest.
Although most commonly eaten as they are, it has become very popular to make avocado toast, combine them in salads, and use them to make scrumptious baked goods - check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our recommended recipes, including a unique avocado chocolate pudding!
As well as being delicious, avocadoes also boast many nutritional benefits: they are an excellent source of fibre, potassium, and folate, all of which support heart and cardiovascular health, and are rich in vitamin E. We also sell frozen avocado flesh! They have the same great flavour and nutritional benefits as fresh avocados we have simply removed the flesh from the skin and frozen it in our warehouse - no colourings, additives, or flavourings have been added.

NAME: Avocado - long neck
Description:
Long Neck avocados are one of the most visually distinctive fruits we sell!
As the name suggests, Long Neck avocados are best known for their shape, which is an entirely natural characteristic. They gained worldwide fame for their unusual shape n 2019 when a photo of these extremely long fruits, which can grow up to 45cm in length, went viral on social media - a chef subsequently revealed that they are so large, you can make 12 avocado toasts from a single Long Neck avocado!
However, these large avocados are also favoured for the wonderful taste of their thick yellow-green flesh, encased by thin, shiny, and smooth green skin. One bite of this creamy and buttery flesh, with its unique salty and sweet flavour, will leave you eager for more!
Like smaller avocados, these fruits too have their cavity filled with a brown seed, but rest assured that the pit is small in comparison to the amount of edible flesh!
Long Neck avocados are best enjoyed when eaten fresh out of hand, but the moisture-dense flesh is also well suited to other raw applications, working well in both sweet and savoury recipes. We'd recommend removing the flesh from the skin, slicing or cubing it, and then adding it to salads, sandwiches, or tacos; layering the flesh over sushi; chopping it into salsa, or mashing it into guacamole. In short, you can use Long Avocados in any of the ways you'd use traditional avocados.
As well as being delectable, Long Neck avocados are an excellent source of fibre and vitamin K, and are rich in potassium, folate, and vitamin C.
The Long Neck avocado has a short season so they are not the avocado of choice for large-scale avocado farmers, so we usually source ours from rare fruit growers who specialise in unusual varieties.

Aside from garnishing, Long Neck avocados are perfect for simply eating out of hand, or why not make your own guacamole with the creamy, buttery flesh?

NAME: Babaco
Description:
Babaco fruits are spectacular fruits that deserve more recognition!
Although they are still mainly consumed in central and South America where they originated (we source ours from Ecuador), the mouthwatering taste of these hybrid fruits - they were created by combining two varieties of papaya (also known as pawpaw) - has enticed fruit lovers from across the world to enjoy their delicious flesh.
They have a unique shape, almost resembling an oblong but with 5 flat sides, cutting into appealing star-shaped slices, and a relatively large size, measuring up to 12 inches long and weighing up to 1.5kg! Once the fruit is fully ripened, babaco's thin, smooth skin takes on an attractive golden-yellow hue, and it is edible too! Underneath the skin is juicy white, seedless flesh that delights the tastebuds: the flavour is multi-layered and distinctive, with both sweet and acidic elements, but eaters distinguish notes of pineapple, kiwi, and its parent fruit papaya. What really makes the flesh stand out is its surprising fizziness - so renowned has this quality become that babaco has gained the nickname 'champagne fruit'!
Delectable when eaten fresh out of hand - remember the entire fruit is edible! - especially when sprinkled lightly with sugar, babaco's versatility means it can also be used in any number of sweet and savoury recipes. We'd recommend pureeing the flesh to create refreshing smoothies or tangy barbecue sauce (simply combine it with brown sugar, wine vinegar, ketchup, pepper, salt or soy sauce, and garlic), optimising its tropical flavour to make wonderful desserts, from pies to ice creams, and mix into salads. Babaco's relation to its parent fruit means it can additionally be utilised in any recipe calling for papaya. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recommended recipes, including a superb banana tiramisu, the ultimate dessert for fruit lovers!
As well as being extremely flavourful, babaco boasts many nutritional benefits too. In particular, babaco is an excellent source of vitamins A and C and is known to promote healthy digestion.

Our fresh banana leaves are also ideal for decoration, adding a visually striking feature to any room, and are the perfect quirky gift for fruit fanatics.

As well as being common sights in photoshoots, they are ideal centrepieces during celebrations too, often being used as a large platter to serve food on! NAME: Banana - burro
Description:
Are you a banana lover looking for a new variety to try? Our burro bananas are just the thing for you!
Burro bananas are primarily cultivated in Mexico and the Philippines, however we source ours from the Caribbean.
The name 'burro' comes from these bananas' short, plump shape, because their stubby stature is reminiscent of a 'burro', the Spanish word for 'donkey'! Indeed, burro bananas are occasionally sold under the name chunky banana as they are stubbier and more square-shaped than the common banana; some are even completely triangular!
The peel is a rich, vivid, dark green that turns deep yellow with characteristic black/brown spots when ripe. When young, the flesh of the burro banana is tart and tangy with notes of apple and lime. As the fruit matures, the yellow flesh is soft on the outside with a slightly crisp, textured centre. A ripe burro banana's flesh wows with its divine flavour: your tastebuds will be delighted by the creamy, sweet flesh with its wonderful lemon undertones!
Burro bananas are known as a dual-purpose variety because as well as enjoying them fresh out of hand when they're fully ripe, they can also be eaten green like a plantain! Burro bananas are also versatile in that they are ideal for use in both sweet and savoury preparations! When they're green, they're perfect for combining into curries and frying into banana chips. When they're ripe, they can be enjoyed in any way you'd consume regular bananas, from making smoothies and sorbets to making scrumptious banana bread! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including amazing burro banana muffins!
As well as being supremely delicious, burro bananas boast numerous nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of potassium and are rich in vitamins B and C, dietary fibre, and magnesium. They also contain good amounts of phosphorous, magnesium, calcium, iron, and zinc. Our frozen, peeled burro bananas are offered in 1kg vacuum packs. They contain on average 11 to 12 bananas per packet. The bananas are frozen ripe so will be soft when defrosted, best used in smoothies.

The bananas are held in cold storage on the ship to prevent ripening and then either ripened in temperature controlled rooms, or artificially ripened with gasses.
The only cavendish bananas we offer are sent to the UK by air so they can be harvested when more mature and once more flavour and nutrition has developed. They can be ripened naturally by you at home.

Although small in size - they are roughly the same size as apple bananas, which are about half the length of Cavendish bananas - these plump 'baby bananas' are far superior to supermarket-bought bananas in aroma, texture, and flavour!
When you peel back the thin, smooth, yellow skin of kolikuttu bananas, you are instantly greeted with a glorious fragrance reminiscent of apples. Your tastebuds will be wowed by the cream-coloured flesh which is divinely soft (indeed, they are also known as 'silk bananas' due to their texture!) and has a perfectly balanced sweet-sour taste profile, with apple-like undertones. This creaminess and brilliant flavour have made them one of the most highly prized dessert banana varieties across Asia! Indeed, they are so highly regarded that they are one of the most commonly chosen fruits for offerings during religious festivals.
Delectable when eaten fresh out of hand, they are also ideal for use in a range of recipes, their unique flavour making them perfect for savoury as well as sweet applications. We'd particularly recommend capitalising on the velvety smooth flesh to make delicious smoothies, but they are also well-suited to baking scrumptious banana bread, adding some fruity goodness to your breakfast, and stirring into curries! NAME: Banana - matoke
Description:
Our matoke bananas from Uganda are a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
These bananas are small to medium in size and are short and plump in shape. They are harvested when they are still green, before they have fully matured - these unripe bananas are perfect for cooking, particularly boiling, steaming, and roasting! Their dense, starchy flesh becomes significantly softer once cooked, and this tender flesh provides distinct sour notes, meaning it is ideal for combining into savoury meals. Indeed, the dish resulting from steam-cooked, mashed matoke bananas is considered a national staple in both Uganda and Rwanda!
Although they are most commonly utilised as green cooking bananas, if you leave the matoke bananas to ripen fully (with the skin becoming a vibrant yellow), you can also enjoy them as dessert bananas, simply eating fresh out of hand as you would with other banana varieties! Once fully mature, the bananas delight the tastebuds with their divine sweetness and subtly bitter aftertaste. The ripe bananas are ideal for use in any sweet or savoury recipe calling for bananas - from banana bread and ice cream to topping porridge and yoghurt, their astounding taste will shine through to make any dish or sweet treat a real delight. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including scrumptious mini banoffee pies!
As well as being delicious and versatile, matoke bananas are nutritionally beneficial. In particular, they are rich in dietary fibre and a good source of protein.

Description:
One of the most widely consumed fruits in the world and a notable 'superfood', plantains are a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
Plantains are slender and elongated in shape and boast a considerably larger size than standard bananas. They have thin, smooth peel and firm flesh.
Green plantains are cooking bananas: their high starch and low sugar content (compared to dessert bananas) mean they have to be cooked to be truly edible. They are primarily incorporated into savoury dishes - they are utilised somewhat like potatoes due to their similarly floury, dense flesh. In fact, they are the chosen plantain for fried plantain chips and can be used in any recipe calling for potatoes! Delicious when fried, boiled, baked, pickled or grilled, it's no wonder that they are extremely popular throughout Western Africa and the Caribbean and that this reliable, all-season fruit is ranked as the tenth most important staple food in the world!
Mature, yellow plantains can be peeled like typical dessert bananas; the pulp is softer than in immature, green plantains and some of the starch has been converted to sugar. They can be eaten raw, but as they are not quite as flavourful as dessert bananas, they are usually cooked. Fully ripe, yellow plantains are ideal for caramelizing: the sweet, golden-brown flesh makes a perfect addition to savoury dishes, as attested by Caribbean (and especially Cuban) cuisines! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including baked plantain empanadas!
If you leave plantains to ripen fully, until the skin turns black and they are soft all over, they develop a divine sweetness and a wonderfully light, fluffy texture with a slight bite, earning them the nickname, 'marshmallow banana'!
As well as being delectable and versatile, plantains provide an array of impressive nutritional benefits too. With more than twenty times the amount of vitamin A, three times the vitamin C, and almost twice the potassium as standard bananas, they are an essential addition to your diet!

NAME: Banana - red (whole racks available)
Description:
Red bananas are a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
We sell both rath kessel red bananas from Sri Lanka and red dacca bananas from Ecuador. Both are similar in shape to (although slightly smaller than) standard yellow bananas, but immediately catch the eye with their dazzling red/maroon rind. You'll notice that rath kessel bananas are more rounded, whereas red dacca bananas have more noticeable ridges.
When you peel back the smooth, thick skin, a fruity scent is released - rath kessel bananas are the more aromatic of the two. When fully ripe, the deep yellow to orange coloured flesh (sometimes with subtle pink hues) is delicately soft and creamy, and it delights the tastebuds with its notes of berry and mango.
Rath kessel bananas are especially delicious. The flesh is softer and smoother than that of most bananas, and the richness of their exotic sweetness is particularly notable. If you're a first-time buyer of red bananas, we'd recommend starting with rath kessel (also known as rath kehel) bananas - we know you won't be disappointed!
Although the mouthwatering tropical sweetness of red bananas means they are best enjoyed when simply eaten fresh out of hand, they are also perfect for use in a range of recipes! Whether you use them to top pancakes or cereal, blend them into smoothies or ice cream, make banana bread, or mellow the spiciness of curries, you'll love these amazing fruits! In fact, you can use red bananas in pretty much any way you'd use yellow ones! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite red banana recipes, including a scrumptious custard and banana pudding!
As well as being delectable, red bananas provide many health benefits. Indeed, they are more nutritious than the popular yellow cavendish bananas commonly found here in the UK, notably containing significantly more vitamin C! In particular, they are rich in vitamin B6, potassium, and dietary fibre, and the rapid energy boost given by their high sugar levels means that they're a great, healthy snack.

NAME: Baobab pod
Description:
With a delicious taste and a 'superfood' status, our baobabs from Nigeria are a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
Although native to Africa, Australia, and Madagascar, baobabs have become globally renowned. These tough brown pods are medium to large in size - often roughly the size of a coconut - and round to oval in shape. Externally, they have firm, velvety shells and brown stems - the shells vary in toughness, some requiring a hammer or other tool to crack them open but others being able to be cracked by hand. Once opened, baobabs reveal many pieces of delicious, dry, cream-coloured pulp encasing hard seeds. The slightly chewy, sweet-sour pulp is either eaten fresh or dissolved in milk or water to make a delightfully refreshing drink, which many people say has a taste reminiscent of lemonade! The seeds can be eaten too and possess a rich, acidic taste somewhat similar to Brazil nuts. The pulp and the seeds are usually eaten separately, as the two have contrasting flavours that taste unpleasant when combined.
Baobabs are praised for their culinary versatility, being perfect for making a range of sweet and savoury food and drink recipes! Although most commonly mixed with milk and honey or sugar to make a sweet and refreshing drink, there are lots of regional variations in culinary use. For example, in Angola, the pulp is usually boiled and the resulting broth is used as the base for a type of ice cream known as gelado de múcua, and in Zimbabwe, the crushed crumbly pulp is stirred into porridge! The pulp can be ground in a powder too which is a perfect ingredient for sauces, jams, and baked goods such as cookies - if you don't want to make your own powder, why not buy some 100% pure baobab powder from our shop? Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including scrumptious baobab muffins!
As well as being delicious, baobabs stand out amongst other fruits in their nutritional value: they are rich in vitamin C, have 4 times the amount of potassium as bananas, and are a great source of calcium!

NAME: Bat nut - fresh and dried
Description:
Bat nuts are native to warm temperate parts of Eurasia and Africa where they have been cultivated for their edible seeds for at least 3,000 years. They grow on floating plants in slow-moving water up to 5m deep.
The ornately shaped fruits resemble the head of a bull or the silhouette of a flying bat. Their striking appearance looks man-made, and upon first glance, many people can't believe they are natural. Each fruit contains a large, starchy seed, which (once boiled) tastes similar to chestnut and firm potato. They're best eaten with a sprinkle of salt.
They're ready to harvest in the autumn and are only available for a short period of time.
In India and Pakistan, bat nuts are known as singhara or paniphal (eastern India) where they are widely cultivated in freshwater lakes. When the fruit has been dried, it's ground into a flour called singhare ka atta, which can be consumed as a phalahar (fruit diet) on the Hindu fasting days, the navratas. The flour is also used for making bread.
Not only are the bat nuts used as food, they are also a popular decorative item. In Southeast Asia, local people wash and polish them and then make various handicrafts including necklaces. Water caltrop are not eaten raw, they are boiled or roasted first.

NAME: Batoko plum
Description:
Our batoko plums from Sri Lanka are a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
Despite their name, bakoto plums (also known as 'lovi-lovi') are not in fact a variety of plum but are rather small berries. These minuscule - they average between 1 and 2cm in diameter! - round to oval-shaped berries somewhat resemble cherries, boasting smooth, glossy, firm skin that catches the eye with its deep red hue. Beneath their taut skin is yellowish-white flesh that is crisp in texture and primarily sour in flavour, although providing subtle sweet notes too. The flesh contains an inedible seed that should be removed before eating.
Although they are edible when raw, batoko plums are not typically eaten fresh out of hand due to their bitter notes. Instead, they are usually utilised for making chutneys, jams, preserves, and syrups. They are also often stewed with sugar to turn these acidic fruits into a sweet dessert! The flesh can additionally be added to smoothies, combined into your morning granola or porridge, and incorporated into your favourite baked goods recipes, from pies and tarts to cobblers and cakes! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some wonderful recipes, including batoko plum jam and even batoko plum wine!
As well as being supremely versatile, batoko plums have been used for centuries in traditional Ayurvedic medicine, and are still today regarded as being nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are rich in dietary fibre and provide a good amount of calcium and potassium.

NAME: Bitter kola
Description:
Did you ever wonder how Coca-Cola got its name? Well, look no further than the bitter kola plant!
Also known as 'bitter cola' or 'Garcinia Kola', bitter kola originates from West and Central Africa, where it has been highly valued in traditional African herbal medicine for centuries! However, it may be more well known today as the original flavouring of Coca-Cola: some of the first recipes for the popular beverage included bitter kola extract!
Inside the orange-sized fruit is a yellow pulp, surrounding four seeds. Whilst they are sometimes eaten, the fruits of the bitter kola plant are extremely sour, so they are usually harvested for the seeds instead.
The seeds are chewed when raw. They have a bitter, wonderfully aromatic flavour, somewhat similar to that of a raw coffee bean with a sweet and peppery aftertaste! Once the pulp has no flavour remaining, you should spit it out.
You can also use the bitter kola to make a delightful tea - check out the 'Further information' tab below for a YouTube video demonstrating how to make this lovely beverage!
Bitter kola are however not consumed as a food source but rather for the multitude of health benefits which it brings. Among its impressive nutritional qualities, bitter kola is believed to be rich in calcium, vitamin C, and iron, and may be beneficial in treating inflammation and diabetes. It's advised to use no more than 2 bitter kola per day, which you should chew and then spit out. Take it after a meal, rather than on an empty stomach.

NAME: Black corn
Description:
Calling all sweetcorn lovers: if you've never tried black corn, now is the time!
In appearance, black sweetcorn (also known as purple sweetcorn) looks the same as the corn on the cob we are all used to - black corn is botanically classified as 'zea mays', which is the same species as regular corn - except instead of bright yellow, the kernels are an eye-catching jet black in colour (some varieties have white kernels whilst they are immature, developing their black colour once they are fully ripe). Black corn grows in elongated cobs, typically reaching around 20cm in length, and is considered a medium-sized variety.
The kernels of black corn are chewy and starchy. Whilst black sweetcorn is not as sugary as modern varieties of yellow corn, it still delights the tastebuds with a subtle, yet wonderful, sweetness. Ideal for bringing some colour to your mealtimes, be aware that if you eat directly from the cob you will get some of the black oils on your fingers as they develop a sticky texture once cooked! However, the messiness is well worth the delicious flavour.
Black corn can be enjoyed in many different ways. It is well-suited to roasting, grilling, boiling and steaming - simply add a knob of butter and a sprinkle of salt and pepper to perfect the flavour! We recommend using black corn in any recipe that calls for yellow corn to add some variety to your diet. Why not grind the kernels into cornmeal and use it to make cornbread, tortillas, and Indian roti bread, or follow Peruvian tradition by boiling the corn to make the summer drink 'chicha morada'? Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including a light black corn salad, the perfect summer dish.
As well as boasting a striking colour that stuns the eyes and a delectable taste, black corn is also supremely nutritionally valuable. It is rich in anthocyanins, a plant pigment that has numerous anti-inflammatory and antioxidant benefits, and also contains important minerals and nutrients such as iron, magnesium, vitamin A, folate, and phosphorus.

NAME: Black sapote 'chocolate pudding fruit'
Description:
For us here in the UK, the black sapote represents the holy grail of fruits. It's no wonder then that it is a clear customer favourite and is one of the most sought-after fruits in the country!
Black sapote are a small to medium-sized fruit which are native to Mexico, Central America, and Colombia, but are now also cultivated in the USA and the Philippines (due to its sensitive nature, it isn't grown commercially on a significant scale, nor is it exported around the world in large quantities). Their shape somewhat resembles Bramley cooking apples and they can be a similar size too. The skin of the fruit is bright green turning to olive green as they mature on the tree, and finally shifts to very dark green to brown once they are ripe and ready to eat. It can be hard to recognise the slight colour change of mature fruits from bright green to olive green. Experienced pickers are needed to ensure only the mature fruits are harvested. In order to reduce disruption to the tree and avoid ripe fruits being knocked and falling to the floor, a long harvest pole with a fabric net is used to cut and pick the fruit.
The glossy dark brown flesh of the fruit is soft, loose and buttery. It's like a really soft, slightly-mashed avocado. There are usually a few medium-sized seeds in the middle of the fruit.
Wondering what the reason is for the excitement surrounding black sapote? A hint lies in its nickname, 'chocolate pudding fruit' - as a nation of chocolate lovers, we're instantly attracted to anything with chocolate in its name! The ripe flesh of black sapote certainly does look like chocolate mousse and has virtually the same texture too. Whilst the flavour is not the same as chocolate mousse, some people do note subtle chocolate-like flavours amongst other wonderful flavours including honey, date and caramel. This heavenly combination makes for a real treat for the tastebuds! We would regard this fruit as medium-sweet to sweet with a subtle delicate flavour.
As well as being delicious, black sapote also boast a number of health benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C, providing more than 6 times the daily requirement! Additionally, they contain good amounts of calcium and phosphorous.

NAME: Blue olive

Our blue olives from Sri Lanka are a must-try!
The small fruits are a type of Ceylon olive. They immediately catch the eye with their nearly perfectly spherical shape and smooth, glossy, bright blue skin. Beneath their appealing skin is firm green flesh that is somewhat reminiscent of avocado in texture. Once fully ripe, this pasty flesh boasts a delicious savour: they have a tangy, sour taste which some say is comparable to that of tangy, Mediterranean olives.
Being pleasingly bite-sized, blue olives are perfect for eating fresh out of hand. However, they are also extremely versatile - they are well-suited for both sweet and savoury applications! In their native Sri Lanka, they are popular ingredients in a variety of recipes: they are boiled and combined with cooked dishes; used to make delectable chutneys and pickles, and often sprinkled in chilli flakes and salt to create mouthwatering snacks! They are also commonly sold by street food carts in the form of the pickle dish veralu achcharu - the olives are boiled, squashed, combined with similarly spectacular exotic fruits such as guava and mango, and finished with a glaze of vinegar, mustard, chilli, and sugar! As well as boasting an appetizing taste and culinary versatility, blue olives have also been used in traditional Sri Lankan medicine for centuries, and today they are still highly regarded for their nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre and, due to their unique blue colour, are exceptionally rich in anthocyanin, an antioxidant that is believed to boost the immune system.

NAME: Breadfruit
Description:
Often referred to as a 'tropical potato', breadfruit is certainly one of the most unusual fruits we sell!
Related to mulberry, fig, and jackfruit, breadfruit is native to many regions across the tropics, and is known for requiring minimal care and bearing fruit much quicker than other plants - its yield can be up to 200kg per year! Breadfruit trees are also drought resistant and can survive tropical storms. It is for this reason that breadfruit is such a staple part of the diet of millions of people!
Large in size and round to oval in shape, breadfruit's pebbled skin matures from green to yellowish-brown and its cream-yellow flesh has, when eaten raw, a custard-like texture and is sweet to taste, with a flavour similar to jackfruit, corn, and durian. Breadfruits are usually, however, cooked before consumption to enjoy a richer flavour and softer consistency - during cooking, they release a sweet and fragrant aroma reminiscent of freshly baked bread, and once cooked, they have a bread-like texture and a taste that resembles potato, artichoke, and chestnut.
Breadfruit can be enjoyed in a number of ways. The flesh can be boiled or steamed and added to pasta salads, mashed with coconut milk or garlic and oil as a side dish, incorporated into pancake batter, or stirred into dips. It can also be added to curries, soups, and stews, or incorporated into casseroles, burritos, rice-based dishes, and falafel.
As well as being delicious, breadfruit is packed full of nutrients. In particular, it is a good source of antioxidants, calcium, dietary fibre, iron, magnesium, omega 3 and omega 6 - you can be confident in knowing that the fruit that's delighting your tastebuds is supremely healthy too!

These white nuts are covered by brown shells and are encased in a white pulp. As the breadnut ripens, the breadnut seed shells become dark brown and develop their characteristically rich flavour. Although not eaten fresh out of hand, once they have been easily removed from the flesh, the seeds can be boiled in salted water, roasted, or steamed. When boiled, their texture is akin to mashed potatoes or hummus; roast them and they'll wow your tastebuds with subtle notes of coffee and chocolate!

As the source of chocolate, cacao is an absolute must-try for exotic fruit lovers and chocoholics alike!
Cacao pods are medium to large in size and oblong in shape. When you open the pod, you will immediately be struck by the astringent, faintly floral aroma of the fruit and see that beneath the dense, textured outer shell are 20-60 compact, elongated seeds (also known as beans) enveloped in a fleshy, white pulp. The delicious pulp surrounding each bean is soft and slippery, whereas the beans tend to be drier and chewier. If you are looking for optimal juiciness, our St Lucian cacao is the best choice, because whilst it has less flesh than the Ecuadorian variety, the pulp is notably more succulent and less dense.
The flavour of cacao pulp and seeds varies depending on the variety and where and how the pods were cultivated, with some notably sweeter than others. However, the pulp typically has a sweet-sour taste, combining fruitiness, tanginess, acidity, and subtle sweetness, with divine notes of pineapple, citrus, lychee, and mango. Some people liken the flavour to 'passionfruit lemonade'! If we were to compare it to other exotic fruits, we'd say that cacao is a unique combination of soursop and mangosteen in texture and taste.
Although most commonly enjoyed by sucking on the glorious white pulp, there are many other ways to make the most of these fruits! For example, you can ferment, dry, and roast the fruit's seeds to turn them into cacao nibs, which are perfect for sprinkling over granola, yoghurt, and ice cream, and can be ground into cocoa powder. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including an article on how to make cacao nibs!
Cacao fruit boasts a host of health benefits. As well as being an excellent source of dietary fibre and vitamins and minerals such as magnesium and potassium, it is the highest plant-based source of iron known to man and has over 40 times the antioxidants of blueberries!

NAME: Carob bean - nature's chocolate
Description:
The carob tree is a species of flowering evergreen tree in the pea family, fabaceae.
It's cultivated for its edible pods. Carob is mildly sweet and is used in powdered, chip, or syrup form as an ingredient in cakes and cookies, and as a substitute for cocoa powder.
Carob consumed by humans is the dried (and sometimes roasted) pod. The pod consists of two main parts: the pulp accounts for 90% and the seeds for 10% of the pod weight.
A traditional sweet, eaten during Lent and Good Friday, is also made from carob pods in Malta. Dried carob fruit is traditionally eaten on the Jewish holiday of Tu Bishvat.
In Cyprus, carob syrup is known as Cyprus's black gold, and is widely exported. In Malta, a syrup (ulepp tal-arrub) is made out of carob pods. This is a traditional medicine for coughs and sore throat. Carob syrup is also used in Crete as a natural sweetener, and is considered a natural source of calcium.
Carob juice drinks are traditionally drunk during the Islamic month of Ramadan.
Carob bars, an alternative to chocolate bars, are often available in health-food stores.
Due to its strong pleasant taste, it can be found mixed with orange or chocolate.
In Libya, carob syrup (called rub) is used as a complement to Asida (Asida is a dish made up of a cooked wheat flour lump of dough, sometimes with added butter or honey. Similar to gruel or porridge, it is eaten in many North African countries.)
Carob contains three times more calcium than milk. It is also rich in iron, phosphorus, and dietary fibre.

Our pure cashew apple pulp is produced from the flesh after the skin has been removed.
The cashew apple is the fleshy part of the cashew fruit attached to the cashew nut. Cashew nuts are well known and more widely traded than the cashew fruits, because the fruits are easily bruised and have a short shelf life.
The top end of the cashew apple is attached to the stem that comes off the tree. The bottom end of the cashew apple attaches to the cashew nut, which is encased in a shell. In botanical terms, the cashew apple is an accessory fruit that grows on the cashew seed (which is the nut).
The cashew apple can have an astringent taste which is sometimes removed by steaming the fruit for five minutes before washing it in cold water.
Cashew apple juice is delicious and has a lot of potential to become a mainstream drink of the future.

The cashew apple can be eaten fresh, cooked in curries, or fermented into vinegar, as well as an alcoholic drink.
It is also used to make preserves, chutneys, and jams in some countries such as India and Brazil.
In many countries, particularly in South America, the cashew apple is used to make juice and flavour alcoholic drinks including cocktails.
In Goa, the cashew apple is mashed and the juice extracted and kept for fermentation for a few days. Fermented juice then undergoes a double distillation process. The resulting beverage is called feni or fenny. Feni is about 40-42% alcohol. The single-distilled version is called urrac, which is about 15% alcohol.
In Tanzania, the cashew apple is used to make a strong liqueur named gongo and in Mozambique, cashew farmers commonly make a strong liqueur from the fruits after they have been left to lose water and ferment. The shrivelled fruits are used for distillation.

NAME: Ceylon olive
Description:
Our Ceylon olives from Sri Lanka are a must-try!
Ceylon olives immediately catch the eye with their nearly perfectly spherical shape and smooth, glossy, green skin. Beneath the appealing skin of these small fruits - they measure only 2.5cm in length! - is firm green flesh that is somewhat reminiscent of avocado in texture. Once fully ripe, this pasty flesh boasts a delicious savour: they have a tangy, sour taste which some say is comparable to that of Meditteranean olives.
Being pleasingly bite-sized, Ceylon olives are perfect for eating fresh out of hand. However, they are also extremely versatile - they are well-suited for both sweet and savoury applications! In their native Sri Lanka, they are popular ingredients in a variety of recipes: they are boiled and combined with cooked dishes; used to make delectable chutneys and pickles, and often sprinkled in chilli flakes and salt to create mouthwatering snacks! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including an olive and ambarella accharu (achcharu), a wonderful Sri Lankan pickle dish!
As well as boasting an appetizing taste and culinary versatility, Ceylon olives have also been used in traditional Sri Lankan medicine for centuries, and today they are still highly regarded for their nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre and provide a good amount of vitamin C.

NAME: Chilli - Bird's eye
Description:
Looking for a new way to add some spiciness to your mealtimes? Bird's eye chillies (also known as 'red Thai chillies') are just the thing for you: although minuscule in size, they pack a punch in flavour!
These chilli peppers historically originated from Mexico but today are most extensively cultivated and consumed in Thailand. They most likely got their unique name from their shape: small and rounded, they resemble a bird's eye! Their smooth, glossy exterior typically ripens from green to an eye-catching bright red. The mature red chillies are fruitier and sweeter than the more bitter, immature green peppers, and they boast a heat rating of 50,000-100,000 Scoville units, making them 10 to 20 times hotter than a jalapeno pepper, which averages around 5000 Scoville units!
Many people find them too hot to eat fresh out of hand. Instead, therefore, these staple ingredients in Thai cuisine tend to be used in small quantities in cooked applications, being ideal for bringing some vibrant colour and a kick of heat to soups, pastas, stir-fries, and curries! They are also perfect for making salsas and marinades, and for grinding into a spicy powder. Make sure to scoop out the small white seeds in the centre of each chilli if you want to reduce the heat intensity. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipes, including one for making peri-peri sauce!
As well as being delicious and versatile, bird's eye chillies provide a range of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and they contain the chemical component capsaicin, which is believed to aid digestion.

NAME: Chilli - scotch bonnet
Description:
Scotch bonnets are a must-try for those looking for a way to add a kick of heat to their mealtimes!
Scotch bonnets are a variety of chilli pepper native to West Africa. They are small in size - average 2-7cm in length - and squat and wrinkled in shape. They have smooth, waxy skin that ripens from green to a vibrant red. Beneath their skin is crisp flesh encasing a cavernous hollow filled with small, flat cream-coloured seeds.
These brilliant peppers have a sweet aroma and a divinely floral, fruity savour with delectable undertones of cherry, tomatoes, and apples! After being delighted by these heavenly flavours, your tastebuds will be wowed by the intense fiery power of peppers, which boast a heat rating of 100,000-350,000 Scoville units! It's no wonder they are also known as 'Jamaican hots'!
Our maroon and deeply wrinkled dried scotch bonnets (packed in 40g bags) are similarly fiery, although the heat from these dried peppers tends to be less immediate and lingers for longer on the palette. They are particularly noted for their smoky savour, imbued with hints of spice and tropical undertones. They can be used in place of the fresh peppers: they are especially perfect for adding heat to raw dishes such as ceviches and their warm, fruity taste works well in combination with mangoes and berries. They also work well when added whole to curries and stews, but make sure to remove them before serving!
Many people will find the fresh peppers too hot to eat by themselves, preferring instead to add a small quantity to their cooking. Indeed, they are staple peppers in Caribbean cooking. They are perfect for boiling, sautéing, and frying, and work especially well when combined into curries, soups, and stews. They are also popularly used to make hot sauces - in Jamaica, they are favoured ingredients for making their famous spicy jerk seasoning! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including wonderful grilled jerk shrimp and pineapple skewers!
As well as being versatile, our 100% natural fresh, dried, and frozen scotch bonnets are also nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are excellent sources of vitamins A and C and magnesium and provide good amounts of flavonoids and phytochemicals.

NAME: Chui jhal
Description:
Looking for a way to spice up your diet? Chui jhal is just the thing!
Chui, also known as 'piper chaba' and 'piper chilli', is a plant native to south and southeast Asia. It is especially valued as a culinary herb in India and Bangladesh. In Bangladesh, it is called 'chui jhal', and is most widely found in the Jashore, Khulna, Satkhira and Bagerhat districts of the country. Chui jhal is one of the most popular spices in southern Bangladesh, and the chopped stems, roots, and skin of the plant are all utilised in cooking and traditional medicine. Indeed, it is one of the most expensive spices you can buy there!
We sell the roots of the plant. They are elongated and thick, with rough brown skin. They have an intense aroma which fills the room, and a strong, spicy taste that makes them ideal for use as a flavouring - they are said to have a taste somewhat reminiscent of horseradish! Perfect for adding some much-needed heat to any number of savoury dishes, in Bangladesh, it is common to incorporate chopped chui jhal roots with meat and fish dishes, especially with mutton and beef curries, to enhance their flavour. Try adding small, chopped pieces 10-15 minutes before the curry is cooked! In Thailand, chui jhal is known as 'dee plee' and is consumed in both fresh and dried forms. It is often ground using a mortar and pestle, and this powder features as an ingredient in a variety of Thai sauces and pastes, as well as soups. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration!
As well as being ideal for bringing a kick of flavour to your mealtimes, chui jhal has been a staple of Ayurvedic medicine for centuries, and is still today believed to boast many nutritional benefits. In particular, it is thought to have anti-inflammatory properties and beneficial phytochemicals. Infusing chui jhal and ginger in boiling water and drinking the resulting soothing herbal tea is believed to help alleviate colds.

NAME: Cinnamon leaves - dried
Description:
The cinnamon tree is known for its thick aromatic bark however the lesser known cinnamon leaves are also sought for their culinary use.
In South Asian and West Indian cooking the leaves are usually added whole to curries, rice dishes and stews to infuse their delicate clove and cinnamon flavour. The leaves are removed at the end of cooking before eating.
The cinnamon leaves are also mixed with hot water to make herbal tea.
As well as their culinary use, the cinnamon leaves are highly regarded for their health benefits. The cinnamon oil, found in the leaves, is known for its stimulating and warming effects on the body which is why the leaves are distilled into an oil for use in aromatherapy and natural medicine. Cinnamon is considered one of the 50 fundamental herbs in Chinese medicine.
The oil is also sought for its powerful aroma and used in perfume.
The naturally occurring oil in the leaves is rich in phytonutrients and contains eugenol which displays antiseptic and analgesic properties that may also contribute to cinnamon's soothing effect. It also has high concentrations of cinnamaldehyde, which has been shown to have anti fungal and antibacterial properties.
The cinnamon tree is a highly versatile plant with many uses - at one time it was considered more valuable than gold.

NAME: Citrus - Beni Madonna jelly orange (luxury fruit for gifting)
Description:
Ehime prefecture in Japan is well known for growing mandarins, but the star of the show is without a doubt the Beni Madonna jelly orange.
Prized for their sweetness and jelly-like softness, Beni Madonna oranges are a sought-after delicacy often given as a gift in the Winter. Their name, Madonna, is believed to be inspired by the nickname for a beautiful character in the famous Japanese novel, Botchan.
Beneath their thin, deep red skin is a flesh that is supremely soft and succulent. As you bite into a jelly orange, the flesh melts in your mouth and explodes with sweetness and a second-to-none juiciness.
First brought to market in 2005, it took farmers over 17 years to first produce them. Much care, dedication and expertise goes into growing a Beni Madonna orange, including control over moisture, covers to protect the soft skin from harsh rainfall and sunlight, and a rigorous selection process where only those passing a high level of sweetness, low levels of acidity and the correct colour are ready for market.
Beni Madonna oranges are a true treat, and unlike any other citrus youll try!

NAME: Citrus - buddha's hand
Description:
Looking for a unique exotic fruit to try? Buddha's hand is just the thing for you!
Buddha's hand, cultivated in Asia for thousands of years, is an unusually shaped citron variety - its fruit is segmented into long finger-like sections, together almost resembling a human hand! The different cultivars and variations of this citron variety form a gradient from "open-hand" types, with outward-splayed segments, to "closed-hand" types, in which the fingers are kept together.
The bumpy, bright yellow (when fully mature) rind is covered with small oil glands that release a divine aroma with notes of lavender and lemon. Unlike other citrus fruits, most varieties of the Buddha's hand fruit contain no pulp, seeds, or juice. Instead, beneath the fragrant, bitter-sweet peel is dense, spongy, white pith with a floral, sweet flavour that will delight your tastebuds.
The peel and pith are primarily used as zest to add tropical flavour to a range of dishes - given its bitter-sweet taste range, it works well in both sweet and savoury recipes! Indeed, we'd recommend using it as an exotic substitute for lemon zest in any recipe calling for a kick of citrus goodness. As well as zesting, the pith and peel can be cut into slices and then used to infuse liquors, olive oils, sugars, and salts. Chopped pith can also be candied to become a sweet chewy treat, turned into mouthwatering marmalades and syrups, or used to flavour tea. If you're looking for a way to really impress people, why not follow Chinese tradition - in China, the Buddhas hand citron symbolises happiness and long life - and cut the pith of Buddha's hand into decorative shapes to (once candied) display as edible centrepieces for dinner parties? Indeed, in Japan, it is a favourite gift for New Year's as it is believed to bestow good fortune on a household! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including Buddha's hand shortbread and a yoghurt and Buddha's hand cake!
As well as being culinarily versatile, Buddhas hand boasts a range of nutritional benefits. In particular, it is a fantastic source of vitamin C and contains dietary fibre (which aids digestion), calcium, and vitamin E.

NAME: Citrus - calamansi
Description:
Love citrus fruit but getting bored of the typical supermarket varieties? Calamansi is just the thing for you!
Calamansi (also known as calamondin) is a small citrus fruit with bumpy green rind and juicy golden-yellow flesh. They are divinely aromatic, with a floral fragrance that fills the room, and their flesh (which contains numerous cream-coloured seeds) has a tart, acidic-citrus flavour that will wow your tastebuds. One thing many people don't know about calamansi is that both the flesh and the rind are edible! The peel has a slightly sweeter taste than the flesh, with satisfyingly tangy undertones.
Calamansi is a versatile citrus that's used in many food and drink preparations. Here in the UK, chefs often use calamansi in dipping sauces and marinades, whilst bartenders use the fruit to make juice, cocktails, and alcohol infusions. It's very commonly used as a condiment in Filipino cuisine like pancit or lugaw, or in the basic sawsawan (dip) of calamansi juice with soy sauce/fish sauce, for fish, spring rolls, dumplings and various meats.
The fruit is used in local recipes in northern Indonesia. Fish are spritzed with the juice prior to cooking to eliminate the "fishy" smell. Kuah asam ("sour soup") is a regional clear fish broth made with calamansi juice. In bars in Asia, it's common for the calamansi to be frozen and used as ice cubes in beverages such as tea, soft drinks, water, and cocktails. A popular liqueur in the Philippines is made from calamansi. Calamansi can also be used to make marmalade and confectionery. As you can see, there are almost endless ways you can use your calamansi - as a place to start, check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes!
As well as being amazingly versatile, calamansi boasts a range of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and have a high content of potassium, vitamin A, fibre, calcium, and limonene, a constituent part of the oil found in the rind that acts like an antioxidant in the way it benefits general health.

NAME: Citrus - cedro diamante, frozen
Description:
Cedro Diamante is a unique citron fruit mostly cultivated in Santa Maria del Cedro, a town named in their honour.
Citron (known in its native Italy as 'cedro') are possibly the first citrus cultivated in Europe, possibly arriving from Persia, and have been cultivated for thousands of years in civilizations around the globe as a culinary ingredient, medicinal remedy, and religious symbol. They are one of the four 'original' citrus fruits, meaning that all other citrus varieties that are in existence today originate from citron. Cedro diamante are particularly important in Jewish culture as the purest and most perfect of all citrus and growing them is a labour of love.
Cedro diamante are one of the largest varieties of citrus, measuring up to three times the size of a supermarket lemon. These immensely aromatic fruits have wrinkled skin that ripens from green to bright yellow, and is enveloped in prominent oil glands, giving the surface a pebbled, glossy appearance. Beneath the skin is a layer of thick, white pith (which constitutes approximately 70% of the entire fruit), encasing a small amount of flesh.
Unlike other citrus fruits, citron has very little juice and flesh, so are most commonly used for their spongy pith and oil-infused zest. The pith is surprisingly sweet and is commonly sliced into small pieces and tossed with sugar and herbs to add some bright citrus notes to salads or combined with balsamic vinaigrette to create a lively salad dressing. The rind has a flavour and fragrance reminiscent of lemons, and In Italy, the peel is customarily candied and enjoyed as a sweet delicacy. The juice of the citron fruit is used as a drink and often as a syrup too. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including a citron risotto!
As well as being versatile and divinely perfumed, citron boast many nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre, potassium, and magnesium, and also provide good amounts of vitamin C, iron, and vitamin B6.

NAME: Citrus - clementine
Description:
Looking for a new variety of citrus to try? Our Spanish leafy clementines are just the thing for you!
Once you peel back the glossy, textured, orange rind of these small to medium-sized fruits (usually 6-7cm in diameter), you will understand part of the reason why they're so highly praised - the way the flesh greets you with a glorious citrus fragrance that fills the room.
However, their flavour is just as divine. The segmented flesh is sublimely juicy and tender, with an intense aromatic taste and powerful notes of acidity that will wow your tastebuds. Wonderfully refreshing, succulent, and flavourful, they are also favoured because they usually contain no seeds (or a few at most), making them easier to eat.
Clementines make the perfect healthy snack, however their uniquely sweet and tart flavour profile also means they are ideal for a range of culinary applications. We'd recommend using them to add a citrus kick to cocktails and mocktails, create scrumptious fruity desserts and baked goods, and complement the sour, earthy notes in curries and meat dishes. Citrus - etrog
Description:
Etrogs are must-try citrus delicacies!
They are a member of the citron family. They have been cultivated for thousands of years but are today one of the rarest citrus fruits around, being grown primarily for traditional Jewish rituals.
Whilst they look somewhat like an oblong lemon, etrogs are considerably larger than their more famous citrus counterpart, averaging 10-15cm in length! They dazzle the eye with both their shape, which can be compared to that of the flame of a candle, and their bright yellow skin.
The glossy yellow rind is thick, bumpy, and immensely fragrant, with a distinctive aroma of lemon and violets. Beneath the rind is spongy white pith that is sweet, yet with slightly bitter undertones. Like other citron varieties, the pith constitutes most of the fruit - etrogs only contain a little bit of pale yellow pulp. This seeded pulp is acidic, but not very juicy.
Etrog's aromatic rind and pith have made them a popular flavouring ingredient by people around the world! The pith and rind are boiled and then simmered in sugar to enhance their sweetness. The cooked etrog is perfect for incorporating into cakes, cookies, and other baked goods, and can also be candied as a sweet treat. We'd particularly recommend simmering etrog into marmalades, jellies, and jams and infusing it into vodka to impart a citrus, floral flavour.
Once defrosted, our frozen etrog can be used in the exact same way as our fresh etrog! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including etrog liquor!
As well as being versatile, etrog are nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are extremely rich in vitamin C and provide a good amount of dietary fibre and potassium. As our frozen etrog is made of 100% fruit, with no flavourings or colourings added, you can be confident in knowing that it is just as healthy as the fresh fruit!

NAME: Citrus - finger lime 'caviar lime'
Description:
Are you looking for an exciting new citrus fruit to try? Look no further than our finger limes, an exotic delicacy!
At first glance, they are seemingly unassuming. They are small in size - they are typically only 4-8cm in length! - and slender (and sometimes slightly curved) in shape, with textured green, pink, or red skin. However, they are enchanting in their minty, citrus aroma, and you will be completely wowed by what's beneath their leathery skin - when you open these wonderful fruits, hundreds of caviar-type globules of citrus goodness spill out! To make them even more eye-catching, as well as emerging in white hues, they are often a vibrant pink or green!
They are not only visually delightful though - they also astound the tastebuds! When you eat them, these pearls of acidic juice (somewhat reminiscent of lime juice) pop satisfyingly in the mouth, releasing a burst of sweet, tangy, and slightly floral flavour as they are chewed. We are sure you will never have experienced anything like this brilliant 'lime caviar', as it has become to be known!
As well as being perfect for eating fresh out of hand, you can layer the pearls over tacos, combine them in grain bowls, green salads, and fruit salads, and sprinkle them (and a dash of sea salt) over sliced avocado or melons to create ideal snacks! Indeed, caviar limes have become widely regarded as superior culinary ingredients - caviar limes are in so much demand from fine dining catering professionals requiring gourmet ingredients that they are currently under development as a potential new widespread commercial crop!
Caviar limes are particularly favoured by chefs because they excel at brightening and perfectly complementing the flavour of seafood such as grilled salmon, seared scallops, sushi, and ceviche. The pearls are also frequently utilized to make delicious marmalades - commercial use of finger limes started in the mid-1990s in boutique marmalades! - and pickles and the fruits are loved by bakers too, as they make supremely attractive cake decorations! Bartenders are similarly enamoured with these special fruits, often using them as fresh, floating garnishes in cocktails and spirits such as mojitos, margaritas, and martinis. Finger lime peel can additionally be dried and used as a flavouring spice. Check out our 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including a brilliant finger lime and elderflower gin fizz!
Alongside being top-quality fruits in their appearance and flavour, finger limes have been used in traditional aboriginal medicines for thousands of years, and are still today regarded as nutritionally beneficial. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and provide good amounts of vitamin E and potassium.

NAME: Citrus - flying dragon orange
Description:
Flying dragon oranges are citrus delicacies that all exotic fruit lovers need to try!
These delicious oranges gained their name from the twisted branches and long thorns of their trees which, when they are bare in the winter, resemble clawed dragons in mid-flight! Due to this eye-catching appearance, the fruit trees are highly regarded as an ornamental variety for private and public gardens, once being planted in the gardens of St Paul's Cathedral!
Flying dragons are native to China and Korea, however they are today cultivated around the world. They are small in size - typically measuring only 3-4cm in diameter! - and round in shape. They have a pebbled, orange rind that has a slightly velvety feel due to their downy coating. Beneath their textured skin is thin, white, spongy pith, attached to tender, yellow flesh that emits a glorious citrus fragrance and is sure to wow your tastebuds: the soft, seeded flesh is exceptionally juicy and intensely tart, astounding eaters with its combination of lemon-like tanginess and bitter notes of grapefruit. These acidic fruits have therefore earned the name 'bitter oranges'!
Like other citrus fruits, flying dragon oranges are not typically eaten fresh out of hand due to their sharp savour and little flesh content. Instead, they are primarily cooked to make delectable marmalades, syrups, jams, and jellies, and are often candied with sugar to create scrumptious chewy snacks! The peels can also be zested like lemons and limes to flavour everything from cakes to cocktails, garnish cocktails (and mocktails!), and create perfect seasoning powder by drying and grinding. A small amount of juice can be extracted from the flesh too which works wonderfully for flavouring alcoholic drinks and desserts such as baked goods and ice cream. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including bitter orange creme brulee!
As well as being versatile, flying dragon oranges are nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are excellent sources of vitamin C and are rich in vitamin A, potassium, and calcium.

NAME: Citrus - grapefruit, pink
Description:
One of the most popular citrus fruits, grapefruits are an absolute must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
Our pink grapefruits are medium to large in size and round - almost perfectly spherical! - in shape. They have attractive golden-orange peel that is smooth, glossy, and semi-thin and is covered with small oil glands that release a delightful floral aroma!
Beneath this fragrant skin is thick, white pith that is bitter and spongy. The pith is attached to segmented flesh that dazzles the eye with its vibrant reddish-pink hue. This tender flesh is supremely succulent, bursting with juice, and boasts a complex flavour profile that combines bright and sweet notes with acidic and tangy undertones!
Although pink grapefruits' sweet-tart flesh is usually simply scooped out and eaten off the spoon, it is also perfect for use in any number of recipes! Ideal for incorporating into fruit and green salads, the flesh is also delectable when blended into smoothies, juiced into cocktails, and chopped into salsas. They are additionally splendid flavouring ingredients, working brilliantly well in imparting tropical notes in baked goods, sauces, and sorbets! As well as being delicious and versatile, pink grapefruits are also nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and are rich in dietary fibre and vitamin A. Our dried pink grapefruit is washed, sliced and dehydrated. There are no added ingredients. Steep it in hot water to make a citrus tea, use in distilling, mix with water and sugar to make your own pink grapefruit syrup, or use for garnishing! For a fruit that is similar to grapefruit, but with a sweeter flavour, we recommend our honey pomelo!

Description:
Jeruk limo is similar to the more well known kaffir lime. They both have a rich green colour, are small and very flavourful. However there are some differences between these two versatile varieties of citrus.
The kaffir lime has a distinctly wrinkled skin and less juice, while jeruk limo has a thick irregular skin, but much more juice than the kaffir lime. Jeruk limo are smaller than kaffir limes.

Jeruk limo are best used before they ripen, when they are still green.

NAME: Citrus - kabosu
Description:
Kabosu is a highly-prized citrus delicacy!
Kabosus are small, round - they are almost perfectly spherical! - citrus fruits that originate from Japan. They have eye-catching dark green peel (ripening to a bright yellow when the fruits are fully ripe) that is smooth, glossy, and covered in small oil glands that emit an intense floral aroma that fills the room!
Beneath this attractive, semi-thin skin is a layer of white, spongy pith that is directly attached to segmented pale yellow flesh. The seeded flesh of kabosu is tender and supremely succulent, almost bursting with juice! This juicy flesh wows the tastebuds with its complex flavour profile: primarily tart and sour in savour, it imparts subtle notes of sweetness too, and impresses with its hints of lemon, mint, and melon.
Closely related to yuzu citrus, it's not surprising that kabosu is similarly perfect for adding a kick of flavour to food and drink recipes! Although in their native Japan kabosu is principally valued for the way its juice mellows the marine-like taste of fish dishes, this acidic juice is extremely versatile. You can use it to create bright, sour-tasting sauces, dressings, and marinades; incorporate it into soups and curries, and infuse it into marmalades, pastries, and even ice cream! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including a scrumptious kabosu lime pie!
As well as being packed full of flavour, kabosus are also nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are rich in vitamin C and are a good source of potassium and folate.
