NAME: Citrus - kagji lebu
Description:
Kagji lebu is a citrus fruit that is extremely popular in its native Bangladesh.
These small, round fruits, which turn from green to greenish-yellow upon ripening, have smooth skin, a strong fragrance, and tangy, succulent flesh. Indeed, the flesh of kagji lebu is said to be even juicier than that of the 'queen of limes', the Bengal-cultivated Gondhoraj lebu!
In Bangladesh, kagji lebu and its sister fruit ada lebu are also used to make chutneys and are commonly cut into pieces or slices and served alongside seafood to give it a sour, fruity note, as well as paired with spicier foods such as curries due to the fruit's complementary coolness. There is also a tradition in Bangladesh to greet guests with a sherbet made from kagji lebu (or Gondhoraj lebu) and palm sugar.
We would suggest using kagji lebu as you would a lemon or lime: squeeze some juice onto your favourite dishes to add a zesty kick to your mealtimes; make delicious, aromatic cocktails and mocktails; combine some zest, rind, and juice into cake and other dessert recipes to bring a citrus profile to baked goods and sweet treats; use as a souring agent for soups and sauces; serve them in wedges - the list is endless! Check out the further information tab for our recommended recipes, including a scrumptious coconut pudding!
Our dried kagji lebu slices are similarly versatile! These dried slices are particularly favoured by chefs, bartenders, and distillers for the tangy kick they impart. They are especially perfect for flavouring and garnishing cocktails, and they make excellent cake decorations too!
Like lemons and limes, kagji lebu are good sources of vitamin C and are rich in many healthful anti-oxidants. Being made from 100% pure fruit, our dried kagji lebu slices provide many of the same nutritional benefits as the fresh fruits, and with no added preservatives, additives, or sweeteners, you can be confident in knowing you're consuming only natural goodness!

NAME: Citrus - key limes, seeded
Description:
Key limes are a must-try for citrus lovers!
These citrus fruits are spherical in shape and small in size, ranging from 2.5 to 5cm in diameter. They have glossy, textured skin that ripens from yellow to an eye-catching deep green with a yellow blush. Beneath their leathery peel is a thin layer of spongy white rind attached to yellowish-green flesh that is tender and incredibly succulent. Key limes have become renowned not only for their intense citrus aroma, but also for the fact that boast a higher acidity than most other lime varieties, which gives them a strong tangy flavour with floral undertones. The flesh contains numerous small white seeds which are inedible and should be discarded.
Although, like other members of the citrus family, key limes are not eaten fresh out of hand, they have many culinary applications suitable for both raw and cooked recipes! With their name derived from their association with the Florida Keys, key limes have become best known as the flavouring ingredient in key lime pie, and we'd recommend using them in other sweet recipes too, such as cakes and ice cream. Their zest and juice are both highly regarded by bartenders and chefs for flavouring cocktails (and mocktails!), jams, marinades, and sauces - indeed, they have become so popular in this sphere that they are sometimes called 'the bartender's lime'! Our dried slices are similarly perfect for flavouring drinks, and make attractive cake decorations and cocktail garnishes too!
As well as being versatile and packed full of flavour, they are nutritionally beneficial too. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and potassium, and are rich in iron and calcium.

NAME: Citrus - kumquat
Description:
One of the most overlooked citrus fruits, kumquats are a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
In appearance, kumquats are comparable to small, oval oranges - indeed, their name comes from the Cantonese term 'kam kwat', which translates to 'golden orange'!
The skin of these olive-sized fruits is thin, glossy, and taut. Beneath the textured, bright orange-coloured peel are 3-6 segments of tender orange flesh, which contain a few small creamish/white seeds. The juicy flesh will wow your tastebuds with its sharp flavour.
However, kumquats stand out amongst other citrus varieties in that the entire fruit is edible, including the peel and the seeds! In fact, the peel boasts a divinely sweet and almost floral flavour, so you experience a fantastic taste sensation of zesty sweetness when you eat kumquats whole!
Although they are often simply eaten fresh out of hand, kumquats' combination of sweet and sour notes means they are perfect for use in both sweet and savoury dishes. Kumquats are popularly utilised in preserves, sauces, and salsas, and we'd especially recommend using them to make scrumptious cakes, pies, and even ice cream! Kumquats are also favoured by bartenders as aromatic edible garnishes and as a bright, fruity flavouring for cocktails and mocktails. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including delicious kumquat marmalade!
As well as being supremely delectable and versatile, kumquats are nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre and are rich in vitamin C.

Indeed, they're so sweet that they have been nicknamed the 'small sugar cannons' of the kumquat family!
These delectable, succulent fruits are best enjoyed fresh out of hand - simply wash the fruits, then devour them! However, honey kumquats are also well suited to a number of culinary applications. NAME: Citrus - lemon, Amalfi, unwaxed
Description:
Looking for a fruit to provide an intense citrus kick to your favourite dishes? Amalfi lemons are just the thing for you!
Native to the scenic Amalfi Coast in Italy, Amalfi lemons are one of the most popular varieties of citrus fruit in Italy and for good reason - they stand out in their delightfully fragrant aroma, abundant juice, and spectacular flavour.
As well as being large in size - they are significantly bigger than supermarket-bought lemons! - Amalfi lemons are also renowned for their distinctive shape, being much more elongated and tapered than the rounder lemons commonly cultivated in Italy.
Amalfi lemons have glossy, yellow peel that immediately attracts the eye. Beneath this bumpy, semi-thick skin is bright white, spongy pith and tender, golden-yellow flesh that will wow your tastebuds: it is supremely succulent and tart with delicate undertones of sweetness. These lemons typically contain a few small seeds encased in their flesh.
Favoured by chefs, our Amalfi lemons are exceedingly refreshing, and their acidic flesh makes their juice the perfect flavouring - they are renowned for having a perfectly balanced juice - whether you are marinading meat or fish, making jams or marmalades, or creating cocktails. Indeed, Amalfi lemons are regarded as the best lemons to use when making limoncello! Whatever you choose, this lemon juice will provide the ideal burst of citrus goodness to anything you desire!
There are more ways to enjoy Amalfi lemons beyond juicing, though! For example, many people are not aware that lemon peel is not only edible, but it is supremely delicious and packed full of nutrients! The peel of Amalfi lemons is extremely aromatic and tangy, and as such, is a wonderful flavouring for creams, liqueurs, cocktails and mocktails, desserts, and more. Their richness in healthy essential oils makes them even more appealing! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite lemon recipes, including a scrumptious lemon and almond cake!
Alongside being packed full of flavour and extremely versatile, Amalfi lemons also offer great nutritional value. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C - they contain even more vitamin C than other lemon varieties! - dietary fibre, and folate, the latter of which is vital for developing healthy red blood cells. Among a range of vitamins and minerals, including potassium and magnesium, these splendid fruits also contain limonene, a natural compound with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.

NAME: Citrus - lemon, Caribbean rough lemon
Description:
Our rough lemons are a rare and unique seeded citrus organically grown on a farm in St Lucia and harvested in the winter months.
The eye-catching uneven exterior is the reason for this variety also being known as 'rough lemon' or 'coarse lemon'.
They are popular across the Caribbean for their thick zest and aromatic juice, which once ripe, is sweeter than other lemon varieties. Being sweeter than the usual commercially available lemons, but still having the usual sour, tart lemon flavour and aroma, rough lemons make a superior lemon juice.
The rough lemons will ripen from green to orange and can be used at all stages of ripeness.
Rough lemons are around two to three times the size of a typical supermarket bought lemon here in the UK.
Some gardeners cultvate rough lemons next to the more attractive meyer lemon, a combination known as 'Beauty and the Beast'.

NAME: Citrus - lemon, meyer lemon
Description:
A cross between a lemon and a mandarin orange, Meyer lemons are a must-try for citrus lovers!
These fruits first cultivated in China resemble other lemon varieties in appearance: they have smooth, golden yellow peel and are round to oval in shape.
Beneath their delicate, supremely aromatic (and edible!) skin is a layer of white pith that is so thin that Meyer lemons may be eaten in their entirety! Not only do Meyer lemons stand out in that they are completely edible: their tender, yellow flesh wows eaters with its distinctive sweet flavour! Unlike other lemons, this often seedless variety possesses little acidity, so the flesh has a sugary taste perfect for those with a sweet tooth!
The bright, floral flavour of Meyer lemons means they are ideal for use in any number of sweet and savoury dishes - Meyer lemons can be used anywhere you want to add pure lemon flavour with none of the characteristic lemon bitterness! We'd recommend cutting thin slices of lemon, removing the seeds, and roasting the slices with root vegetables or seafood. In sweet foods such as marmalade or lemonade, the lower acid level of Meyer lemons means less sugar may be required! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including Meyer lemon marshmallows!
As well as being delicious and versatile, Meyer lemons boast many nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and are rich in potassium.

The bright, floral, and slightly tangy flavour of sweet lemons means they are ideal for use in any number of sweet and savoury dishes. Indeed, sweet lemons can be used anywhere you want to add pure lemon flavour with none of the characteristic lemon bitterness! We'd recommend juicing them to make brilliant marinades and vinaigrettes and candying the peels to create delectable treats. Sweet lemons have been used in traditional medicine for hundreds of years (particularly medicinal beverages for cold and flu) and are still today noted for their nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and are rich in vitamin A, dietary fibre, and potassium.

Description:
Looking for a fruit to provide an intense citrus kick to your favourite dishes? Sorrento lemons are just the thing for you!
Native to the scenic Sorrento Peninsula, waxes, Sorrento lemons are one of the most popular varieties of citrus fruit in Italy and for good reason - they stand out in their delightfully fragrant aroma, abundant juice, and spectacular flavour.
Medium to large in size - they can grow up to 8 times the size of an average supermarket-bought lemon! - and elliptical in shape, Sorrento lemons have glossy, vibrant yellow peel that immediately attracts the eye. Beneath the bumpy, semi-thick skin is bright white, spongy pith, clinging to 10-12 segments of delicate, golden-yellow flesh. These lemons are usually seedless, but sometimes contain a few small seeds.
Favoured by chefs, our Sorrento lemons are exceedingly refreshing, and their tart, acidic yet subtly sweet flesh makes their juice the perfect flavouring - they are renowned for having a perfectly balanced juice which is almost sweet - whether you are marinading meat or fish, making jams or marmalades, or creating cocktails (bartenders are known for preferring Sorrento lemons to other citrus when making gin and tonic and, as the name suggests, they are perfect for making limoncello!). It will provide the ideal burst of citrus goodness to anything you desire!
There are more ways to enjoy Sorrento lemons beyond juicing, though! For example, many people are not aware that lemon peel is not only edible, but it is supremely delicious and packed full of nutrients! The peel of Sorrento lemons is extremely aromatic and tangy, and as such, is a wonderful flavouring for creams, liqueurs, cocktails and mocktails, desserts, and more. Their richness in healthy essential oils makes them even more appealing! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite lemon recipes, including a Sorrento lemon cheesecake, the ultimate dessert!
Indeed, Sorrento lemons offer great nutritional value. In particular, they are a brilliant source of vitamin C, dietary fibre, and folate, the latter of which is vital for developing healthy red blood cells. Among a range of vitamins and minerals, including potassium and magnesium, these splendid fruits also contain limonene, a natural compound with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.
Fun fact: during the twentieth century, Sorrento lemons were sold individually and could only be handled by women who had trimmed nails and wore cotton gloves!

NAME: Citrus - lemon, sylheti jara
Description:
Sylheti jara are delicious, aromatic fruits exclusively cultivated in the Sylhet region of Bangladesh.
Although they somewhat resemble both limes and lemons, these fruits are in fact neither, although they are part of the citrus family.
Fully grown, sylheti jara are quite large, usually boasting a much bigger size than a lemon we see in UK supermarkets. It's not uncommon for this specialty citrus to weigh as much as 1kg each!
However, it is the flavour of these citrus fruits that makes them so sought after. Whereas its sister fruit, the jara lemon, is often completely sour, sylheti jara have a delightfully unique taste that is both sweet and sour.
Although sylheti jara have more pith than the jara lemons, which have a higher proportion of flesh and juice, the floral aroma and delectable taste of the former are considered superior.
Sylheti jara are used in similar ways to jara lemons - to add a citrus kick to mealtimes! For instance, it is common in Bangladesh to pair both of these fruits with spicy dishes, especially in order to impart a sour, citrusy note to curries, and it is also popular to eat the flesh alongside seafood. Some people use it in drinks making too, in particular the creation of liqueurs.

Description:
Dried black limes are a must-try!
Dried black limes are limes which have lost all water content, usually after having spent the majority of their drying time in the sun.
Strongly flavoured, they taste sour and citrusy like a lime but they also taste earthy and somewhat smoky and lack the sweetness of fresh limes. As they are preserved, they also have a slightly bitter, fermented flavour, but the bitter accents are mainly concentrated in the lime's outer skin and seeds.
Given their unique flavour, they are primarily used to add a sour flavour to dishes, through a process known as souring. However, dried black limes have proven to be very versatile, suiting a number of culinary applications, whether you slice, crush or ground them into a powder. For example, in Persian cuisine, dried black limes are used to add this earthy, sour flavour to stews and soups. Across the Persian Gulf they are paired with fish, whereas in Iraq they are added to almost all dishes and stuffing. They are also commonly made into a warm drink called hamidh. Powdered dried lime is also used as an ingredient in Persian Gulf-style baharat (a spice mixture which is also called kabsa or kebsa). Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our recommended recipes, including one for a dark chocolate and Persian lime tart!
As well as being full of flavour, dried black limes also boast a range of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are good sources of vitamin C, potassium and iron.

NAME: Citrus - lime, kaffir lime
Description:
Kaffir limes are citrus delicacies that all exotic fruit lovers need to try!
The kaffir lime is a wonderfully aromatic citrus fruit native to various Asian countries. They are small in size - slightly smaller than regular limes - and round in shape, with a slightly protruded nozzle at the top. They immediately attract the eye with their bumpy, dark green rind. Beneath their appealing skin is a thin layer of spongy white pith, attached to segmented light green flesh. This tender flesh boasts a much richer, more complex flavour than supermarket-bought limes, wowing with its combination of tangy and floral notes.
Although, like other citrus fruits, kaffir limes are not eaten fresh out of hand, their outstanding savour and aroma have led chefs and bartenders around the world to prize them as superior culinary ingredients! Their aroma is so renowned that their essential oil is used in perfumery! They are particularly popular in Southeast Asian cuisine, with the juice, peel, and leaves all utilised in cooking - indeed, in Cambodia, the entire fruit is crystallised/candied for eating! The peel is commonly utilised in marinades and incorporated in Lao and Thai curry dishes to add a fresh, astringent flavour. The zest of the kaffir lime, referred to as combava, is also used in creole cuisine to impart flavour in infused rums and rougails in Martinique, Réunion and Madagascar, and slices of kaffir lime make the perfect cocktail garnishes! We'd particularly recommend using these tantalisingly tart fruits in stir-fries and soups, as well as adding a squeeze of lime juice into a glass of spring water to create an invigorating beverage!
Alongside being supremely versatile and ideal for adding a sharp, zesty kick to your mealtimes, kaffir limes are also nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are excellent sources of vitamin C - one lime provides 32% of your daily vitamin C needs! - and are rich in dietary fibre.

Melogold grapefruits, known in botanical terms as Citrus grandis × Citrus paradisi, are hybrid fruits, developed in the 1980s by crossing a pomelo with a white grapefruit. They are large in size, typically being about 13cm in diameter, and physically resemble their parent fruits: they are round with a somewhat flattened base, with smooth, thin, glossy peel that matures from green to a dazzling bright yellow (although even when they are fully ripe they might still bear some green patches).
The intense, fragrant aroma of melogold grapefruits entices you in, and the taste does not disappoint! Peeling back the skin, you will find a thick white rind encasing 12-14 segments of golden-hued translucent flesh. One bite of the juicy, soft, and tender flesh is enough to wow your tastebuds: a wonderful sweetness perfectly balances the tartness, making them appealing to both lovers of traditional citrus fruits, with their strong tangy flavour, and those who prefer fruits with a more mild taste (indeed, the 'melo' part of their name comes from the fact that they have a 'mellow' flavour when compared to their parent fruits).
Much less bitter and acidic than grapefruits, they are best eaten fresh out of hand so you can enjoy their succulent, sweet-sour flesh. However, melogold grapefruits are also well suited to a number of culinary applications. We'd recommend adding segments to your fruit salads or using them as a brilliant fruity topping for icecream, muesli, and yoghurt; stirring melogold peel zest into your sauces, soups, and stir-fries to impart the fruit's subtle citrus flavour to these savoury items; simmering the flesh into marmalades and jams; chopping the segments to make a unique salsa, or pressing the fruit to make refreshing juice. NAME: Citrus - mikan orange (Spain)
Description:
Mikan oranges are citrus delicacies that all exotic fruit lovers need to try!
Mikan oranges are most closely associated with Japan, where they are highly regarded as speciality fruits. Indeed, they were once so valuable in Japan that they were used as a form of currency there!
They are small to medium in size - typically measuring only 6-8cm in diameter - and round in shape. They have pebbled, reddish-orange rind that is delicate and easy to peel. Beneath their textured skin is very thin, white, spongy pith, attached to tender orange flesh that emits a glorious fragrance and a flavour that is sure to wow your tastebuds. The soft flesh - which is usually seedless but can sometimes contain a few ivory seeds - is exceptionally juicy, and astounds eaters not only with its almost melt-in-the-mouth consistency, but also with its rich savour which combines both sweet and tangy notes!
Unlike other citrus fruits, these supremely refreshing, succulent oranges are best enjoyed when eaten fresh out of hand. Yet, they are also extremely versatile, perfect for use in both sweet and savoury recipes! They are particularly ideal for making delectable marmalades, syrups, and jellies, and are often dipped in chocolate and used as a garnish for desserts! They can also be chopped into salsa and made into sorbet, and their juice is favoured by bartenders as a superior flavouring ingredient for cocktails! In Japan, Mikan peels are dried and ground into a powder which is used in a variety of ways: most commonly, the powder is infused in hot water and honey to create a comforting herbal tea. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including delicious mikan orange jam!
As well as being versatile, mikan oranges have been utilised in traditional medicines for centuries, and are still today valued for their nutritional benefits. In particular, they are good sources of vitamin A, dietary fibre, and potassium.

Description:
One of the most highly-prized pomelo varieties, our madou pomelos from Taiwan are a must-try!
These pomelos get their name from the primary place where they're cultivated - the Madou region of Taiwan. Taiwan is said to pride itself on the quality of its pomelos: in fact, the Madou Farmer's Association holds a pomelo beauty contest every year! It's perhaps unsurprising then that Madou alone accounts for nearly 30% of Taiwan's annual exports of pomelos.
Like other pomelo varieties, madou pomelos are large in size - pomelos are, after all, the biggest citrus fruit in the world, with a single fruit sometimes weighing up to 5kgs (however most export-quality fruits are around 1-2kgs). Although their rounded shape means that at first glance they resemble grapefruits, pomelos (also known as shaddocks, after the sea captain who brought them from Polynesia to the West Indies) are actually a species in their own right.

Beneath their textured, glossy, easy-to-peel skin (which ripens to a yellowish-green) is firm golden-coloured flesh that will dazzle your tastebuds: one bite of the supremely juicy, segmented flesh, with its notable sweetness (and subtly sour undertones) is enough to make you a fan! Although the pith around the segments is bitter and therefore not usually eaten, the fact that the flesh is almost seedless means you have more mouthwatering fruit to enjoy.
Whilst pomelos are usually eaten raw to enjoy the explosion of sweet-sour succulence that their flesh offers, because they are the least acidic of all citrus fruits, they are well-suited to a number of recipes! We'd particularly recommend using them to add some exotic flavour to your salads, chopping them into salsas, blending them into smoothies and pressing them for their richly flavoured fruit juice that will liven up your cocktails (or mocktails!) They can also withstand heat, so they are ideal for simmering into jams and compotes, incorporating into baked goods recipes, and roasting in the oven topped with unsalted butter. As well as being delectable, madou pomelos are nutritionally valuable too. In particular, they boast a high concentration of vitamins A and C, and are a good source of potassium and copper.

These plump fruits have thin, pebbled, green rind that sometimes gains an attractive yellow/orange blush when the fruits are fully ripe. Beneath their textured, wonderfully aromatic skin is segmented, tender, yellowish-orange flesh that is sure to wow your tastebuds: the soft, usually seeded (although sometimes seedless) flesh is exceptionally juicy, bright, and tart. The acidic juice is ideal for flavouring sauces, noodles, meats, and fish dishes, and also works well in alcoholic drinks and desserts such as baked goods and ice cream! In Okinawa, for instance, shikuwasa juice is combined with awamori, a local alcohol, to create a powerfully pungent drink which astounds with its sweet and sour hues. We'd recommend simply squeezing a splash of juice into a glass of spring water to create an invigorating morning beverage! The peels can additionally be zested like lemons and limes to flavour everything from cakes to cocktails and they are popularly used as garnishes too. NAME: Citrus - sudachi
Description:

Cultivated primarily on the Japanese island of Shikoku, sudachi are extremely popular and highly prized in their native Japan - they are beginning to become globally renowned too, as chefs and bartenders seeking gourmet delicacies are starting to recognise sudachi's potential to enliven a range of food and drink recipes!
These premier culinary ingredients are small in size - measuring only 3-4cm in diameter! - round in shape. Harvested when dark green, their thin, leathery, textured skin becomes a delightful golden-yellow upon ripening. Although supremely visually attractive, sudachi are primarily renowned for what's beneath their peel: their succulent, orange-yellow flesh. Their tender, seeded flesh emits an intense citrus aroma and is highly regarded for its high juice content.
Like other citrus fruits, sudachi are not usually eaten out of hand. Instead, they are principally used for their juice - the juice's fragrant perfume and delightfully sour, peppery taste, offering distinctly herbal undertones and a much zestier flavour than lime or lemon juice, makes it the perfect flavouring! Similar to yuzu juice, sudachi juice works well in both sweet and savoury recipes, adding a tart, tangy kick to drinks (especially cocktails!) and desserts but also pairing well with meats, fish, sushi, ceviche, salads, and much more! Sudachi juice is famously considered essential when eating matsutake mushrooms and is commonly used to make ponzu sauce, a delicious Japanese dipping sauce. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including chunky sudachi cookies and a brilliant sudachi margarita!
A great source of calcium, iron, and dietary fibre, and with a higher vitamin C content than lemons, sudachi juice is not only extremely appetizing but will be a very healthful addition to your diet too!

NAME: Citrus - tachibana orange
Description:
Tachibana oranges are citrus delicacies that all exotic fruit lovers need to try!
Tachibana oranges are native to Japan, where they are highly regarded as speciality fruits. Indeed, they have been revered since ancient times - they are one of the country's oldest citrus fruits! - and used to be one of the most favoured fruits of the Japanese royal family. Aristocratic women even used to perfume themselves with tachibana in lieu of bathing!
They are small to medium in size and round in shape, with pebbled, orange rind that is delicate and easy to peel. Beneath their textured skin is thin, white, spongy pith, attached to tender orange flesh that emits a gloriously zesty and subtly spicy fragrance. The soft, seeded flesh is juicy and boasts a richly sour savour, with very subtle undertones of sweetness.
Like other citrus fruits, these succulent oranges are not typically eaten fresh out of hand due to their sharp savour. Instead, they are primarily cooked to make divine marmalades, syrups, jams, and jellies! Tachibana juice is also perfect for adding an acidic kick to soups, stews, and curries, and making tachibana tea is beginning to become popular in Japan. The oranges are also in great demand among bartenders and distillers - they are regarded as gourmet ingredients because their peels are particularly adept at flavouring cocktails (and mocktails!), gins, and other alcohols, as well as being brilliant garnishes!
As well as being versatile, tachibana oranges have been utilised in traditional medicines for centuries, and are still today valued for their nutritional benefits. In particular, they are good sources of vitamin A, dietary fibre, and potassium.

NAME: Citrus - tangelo
Description:
Love oranges but getting bored of the same supermarket varieties? Tangelo may be just the fruit for you!
Tangelos are the result of a hybridisation between a tangerine and a pomelo. Medium to large in size - they are usually about the size of an adult's fist - tangelos' shape catches the eye, owing to the distinctive protrusion at the top of each fruit. Their thick, pebbled, dark orange skin is loose and easier to peel than standard oranges, and their seedless flesh (in 10-12 sections) is incredibly succulent and refreshing, with a delectable flavour that is tangy and tart, complemented by a medium sweetness.
Although most often eaten fresh out of hand, tangelos' sweet yet tart flavour means they are incredibly versatile, being ideal for use in a variety of sweet and savoury food and drink recipes. You can use tangelos for any recipe that calls for oranges or tangerines, but we'd especially recommend: using them to make invigorating juice, to be drunk by itself or put in cocktails, smoothies, and sauces to give them a tangy citrus kick; adding segments to salads to infuse them with some exotic fruit flavour; making salsas to accompany seafood dishes, and zesting them to bring some freshness to sweet desserts. Even tangelos' peel can be used, most often simmered in a sugar syrup to make candied peel! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes.
Our dried tangelo - dried fruit and dried peel - is perfect for cocktail garnishing or infusing hot and cold water to create the ideal, aromatic drink! Meanwhile, our 1kg vacuum bags of frozen peeled tangelo are perfect for making your own tangelo juice!
As well as being delicious, tangelos boast a number of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C, providing almost 60% of the required daily amount! They are also rich in dietary fibre, folate, and calcium.

NAME: Citrus - UGLI® fruit
Description:
UGLI®* fruit is a type of tangelo, which is a variety of citrus fruit. They're grown exclusively in Jamaica and come in different sizes varying in diameter from 4 inches to 6 inches and many varieties of colour from green to greenish-yellow, to yellow, and some even orange! They are only harvested and sent to market after they have ripened on the tree, so what is found in the store is always ripe fruit even though the skin may be green. Inside, the flesh is always orange to deep orange.
It was discovered growing wild in Jamaica over 80 years ago. The original tree is believed to have been a hybrid formed from the Seville orange, the grapefruit and the tangerine families.
The fresh flavour of UGLI® fruit is delicious in many recipes, adding a subtle tang to both sweet and savoury combinations. It is exceedingly juicy, and has a flavour that does not need added sugar unless you have a very sweet tooth. The simplest way to serve the fruit, is to cut them in half, loosen the segments, and eat with a spoon - this is a delicious breakfast dish.
UGLI® fruit are remarkably juicy, and squeeze easily for refreshing drinks. A glass of ugli fruit juice makes a refreshing, flavourful change to fresh squeezed orange or grapefruit. The juice is also delicious warmed as a hot toddy with rum, and sweetened with honey or brown sugar.
When buying the UGLI® fruit, do not be misled by their appearance, you will love their sweet and tangy flavour!

NAME: Citrus - vanilla orange
Description:
If you are an orange lover looking for a new variety to try, vanilla oranges are the perfect option, especially as they are grown in Italy using organic growing methods.
Neither a blood orange or a navel orange, vanilla oranges are a distinct variety belonging to the blonde orange family and are characterised by their distinct lack of navel and quintessential sweetness reminiscent of vanilla!
They are a medium sized variety with delicate orange skin and a thin peel. Beneath their smooth skin is a bright orange flesh that is low in both acid and sugar, making them notably less sour than other citruses.
Their sweetness means vanilla oranges are best enjoyed out of hand. However, they are also perfect for incorporating into sweet and savoury recipes. They are particularly good for pressing into juices due to their high juice content and incorporating into desserts due to their intense smell.
As well as being delicious and versatile, vanilla oranges are nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre and vitamin C.

NAME: Citrus - yuzu
Description:
Need a new citrus fruit to try? Look no further than yuzu, premier culinary ingredients that will add a kick of flavour to your mealtimes!
These extremely sought-after citrus fruits originated from China and Tibet. It was introduced to Japan and Korea during the Tang Dynasty and it is in these nations that today it is most widely cultivated. In these places, yuzu is highly regarded not only for its culinary uses but also for its skincare benefits. Indeed, in Japan, taking a yuzu bath is an annual tradition!
These Asian delicacies have become globally renowned too, as chefs and bartenders seeking gourmet delicacies are starting to recognise sudachi's potential to enliven food and drink recipes!
Yuzu look somewhat like small - typically measuring 7-12cm in diameter - grapefruits with pebbled yellow skin. Although supremely visually attractive, they are primarily favoured for what's beneath their peel: their succulent, yellow flesh. Their tender, seeded flesh emits a zesty, floral aroma and boasts a high juice content.
Like other citrus, yuzu are rarely eaten fresh out of hand. Instead, they are principally used for their juice - the juice's delightfully tart taste, offering distinct notes of grapefruit and mandarin orange and a much zestier flavour than lime or lemon juice, makes it the perfect seasoning! The juice works well in both sweet and savoury recipes, adding tangy notes to drinks (especially cocktails!) and desserts and pairing well with meats, fish, salads! Yuzu is also an integral ingredient in the citrus-based sauce ponzu, and you can additionally use the fruits to make yuzu vinegar. As well as this, yuzu is often combined with honey to make yuzu hachimitsu, a kind of syrup that is used to make yuzu tea or as an ingredient in alcoholic drinks such as the yuzu sour. In Japanese cuisine, yuzu's fragrant zest is used to garnish both sweet and savoury dishes. As well as being versatile, yuzu are known for their various nutritional benefits. In particular, they are rich in fibre, are an excellent source of vitamin C - they contain 3 times more vitamin C than lemons! - and also provide a good amount of iron and calcium.
Our 100% pure dried yuzu is a healthy treat too! Made simply through the process of dehydration, with no added colours, flavourings, or additives, our intensely fragrant dried yuzu is perfect as an exotic garnish for your cocktails and makes a delicious yuzu tea once infused with hot water. You can also remove the seeds and grind the dried yuzu down into a powder which is ideal for adding a unique kick of citrus flavour to everything from chocolate ganache and grapefruit sorbet to grilled white fish, tabbouleh salads and BBQ prawns!
Love yuzu? Take a look at our luxury Japanese Yuzu for the best yuzu you'll ever taste. Are you interested in purchasing yuzu plants? We have yuzu plants here in our tropical greenhouse which we've grown from seed! Please email us to place an order.

NAME: Coconut - mature
Description:
The image that appears in most people's minds when they think of coconuts, round, brown, hairy, and with bright white flesh - these are mature coconuts (so-called to distinguish them from the distinctive young coconut variety).
Coconuts, the fruit of coconut palms - coconut palm trees are native to southeast Asia and islands between the Pacific and Indian oceans, but are believed to be the most widespread fruit trees in the world! - have a variety of culinary uses. For instance, they provide two delicious beverages to enjoy: coconut water and coconut milk.
Once you've punctured the 'eyes' of the coconut using a hammer or corkscrew (see the 'Further information' tab below for more detailed instructions), you can pour the water straight out of the fruit: fresh coconut water has a unique, crisp flavour, incorporating sweet, salty, and nutty notes, and is the perfect beverage to refresh yourself. Coconut milk on the other hand is extracted by pressing the raw, grated meat of the fruit, and because of this it has a similar taste to the meat itself, and a texture someway between the water and thick coconut cream.
Coconut oil is also extracted from the meat of the fruit, and is often used in cooking as a substitute for other vegetable oils. The meat itself is also consumed: the firm white flesh is slightly sweet and is popularly eaten both fresh and dried, as well as grated and shaved, and then incorporating the shavings in a number of recipes, from baked goods and ice creams, to garnishing fruit salads and drinks.
The fresh and dried meat, milk, and water of the coconut can too be used in a variety of food and drink recipes, especially as their unique blend of flavours allows them to work in both sweet and savoury dishes. For example, coconut milk is frequently used to thicken and add a distinctive flavour to soups, sauces, and stews; the raw flesh pairs well with meat and fish dishes, as well as creating delectable sorbets and desserts, and the coconut water is perfect for making exotic cocktails and mocktails! Check out the 'Further information' tab to find some of our favourite recipes, including sweet potato and coconut soup, coconut fish curry and rice, chocolate coconut brownies, and coconut water lemonade!
As well as being versatile and delectable, eating or drinking coconuts in these ways also boasts a range of nutritional benefits. For instance, they are an excellent source of manganese, which is important for bone strength, and copper, are rich in protein and iron, and provide powerful antioxidants.

NAME: Coffee cherry
Description:
Everyone knows coffee, but what about the berry where the famous coffee bean starts out?
The coffee bean is not a bean, but rather a seed, encased in the bright red coffee cherry. Beginning as a green, unripe berry, the fruit gradually ripens to a beautiful deep red at which point it is harvested for it's famous beans. But what happens to the fruit left behind?
Coffee cherries are grown in the 'coffee belt' in places like Brazil, Ethiopia, Columbia and Vietnam. In a lot of places - and particularly amongst coffee farmers in Latin America - cascara tea is made from the dried coffee skin and pulp as a way to use all of the fruit and maximise harvests.
But did you know that the pulp of a ripe coffee cherry can be eaten? Before coffee beans were extracted and roasted, African tribes mashed the coffee cherries with animal fat to create a quick energy source. Though, the taste may be suprising to those expecting something similar to brewed coffee! Under their smooth and glossy skin is a fresh and juicy pulp often compared to a watermelon or apricot. They have a lovely sweet taste with a little bit of tartness, like a tropical fruit.
As well as being versatile, coffee cherries boast many nutritional benefits. They are rich in calcium, magnesium and iron and many class cascara tea - made from the skins of the sweet coffee cherry - as a superfood due to its inflammatory and anti-oxidant properties! Please note that each batch includes a mix of green, orange and red coffee cherries.

NAME: Coffee leaves - dried
Description:
Looking for a new herbal drink to enjoy? Our coffee leaves are just the thing for you!
Coffee leaves are picked from coffee plants, lush, leafy plants plants native to areas of Africa and Asia. Pickers make sure to select only the most pristine young leaves - this is crucial, as it is the youngest leaves that offer the best flavour.
Once the leaves have been cleaned, oxidised, and dried, they are ready to use! The most popular way of enjoying coffee leaves is to make coffee leaf tea.
Coffee leaf tea has been enjoyed for centuries across the world, from India to Jamaica. In Ethiopia, for instance, it was traditional practice to steep the leaves in boiling water for at least 30 minutes, as it was believed that the longer the leaves were boiled for, the sweeter the resulting brew would be. Whilst in Ethiopia it was common practice to add a dash of sugar or salt to the beverage, other cultures added bamboo and sometimes an egg may be stirred in!
For first time drinkers, however, we'd recommend simply breaking up 2-3 coffee leaves into small pieces, steeping them in boiling water for a few minutes, and then consuming! Other popular additions to the drink include sugar, milk, and ginger.
Despite its name, coffee leaf tea is technically not tea - all 'true' teas are derived from the Camellia sinensis tea plant - and it doesn't taste like coffee! Instead, as you sip the silky smooth drink, you will be wowed by its combination of rich, earthy notes and sweet undertones, including hints of vanilla and honey.
As well as being delicious, coffee leaf tea has been regarded as a herbal remedy for hundreds of years, and is still today lauded as supremely nutritious. In particular, it's packed full of antioxidants, boasts anti-inflammatory properties, and has a lower amount of caffeine than both tea and coffee.

Description:
With nicknames such as 'mouse melons' and 'mini watermelons', it is no secret that cucamelons are much smaller than the typical melon. Yet, what these healthful little Latin American fruits lack in size - being bitesize means they are perfect for snacking! - they more than make up for in flavour.
As one of their given names hints at, in appearance they resemble tiny green watermelons, and cucamelons have a similarly delightful tropical aroma, however in other respects they are comparable to cucumbers (hence the 'cuc' part of their name). For example, like cucumbers, they have crunchy, translucent flesh that is full of seeds, and cucamelons have a similar flavour, although the delicate, fresh sweetness is complemented by a delicious citrus kick and faint sour notes - this has led people to say that eating a cucamelon is like eating cucumber drizzled in lime juice.
Although often eaten whole out of hand, the combination of sweet and sour flavours makes cucamelons ideal for savoury as well as sweet recipes: we particularly recommend pickling them to really bring out their crispness; adding slices cucamelon to salads and stir-fries to bring some juicy crunch, and making the most of cucamelons' natural lime taste to use them to make tangy cocktails (look at our 'Further information' tab for recipes)!
As well as being refreshing and flavoursome, cucamelons also have nutritional benefits. They are rich in antioxidants and are an excellent source of fibre, vitamins A and C, and potassium, so they are all around the perfect healthy and ideal way to add some flavour to your mealtimes!

NAME: Damson, frozen
Description:
Damsons are a must-try for fruit lovers!
Damsons are very similar to plums, particularly in appearance - both of these stone fruits are round in shape (although damsons are slightly more oval) and have smooth, eye-catching, blue-purple skin.
Yet, damsons are far superior to supermarket-bought plums in various ways! Many people prefer damsons due to their unique flavour. Whereas plums are sweet fruits, the yellow flesh of damsons will wow your tastebuds with both sweet and sour notes. Their drier, firmer flesh (stemming from a lower water content) also means that it's much easier to remove the stone from damson fruits.
Although they can be eaten fresh out of hand, damsons are usually cooked in order to mellow the flesh's astringent undertones - indeed, their texture and delectable flavour make them well-suited to a number of recipes. From being simmered into jams and jellies or baked into pies, tarts, and cakes (they make brilliant cake toppers as they don't disintegrate when cooked, meaning they retain their shape), to being incorporated into pork casseroles, damsons are wonderfully versatile! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for recipe inspiration, including a scrumptious damson crumble and damson gin, the perfect evening tipple!
As well as being delicious and versatile, damsons also boast a number of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre, are rich in vitamins C and K, and provide a good amount of antioxidants.

NAME: Dates - amir
Description:
Love dried fruit? Amir dates are just the thing for you!
Amir dates, also known as 'Amir Hajj' dates, are renowned throughout the world for their high-quality appearance, texture, and flavour. Indeed, they are reputed to be the best dates in Iran, and across the Middle East they have earned the nickname 'the visitor's date', due to them being considered a delicacy worthy of presenting to guests as a gift (or to be carefully picked and boxed for the export market).

Their sublime flesh is so soft and smooth that it almost resembles caramel, and the flavour is nothing short of mouthwatering. Divinely delicate and rich, they will wow your tastebuds with their notes of cinnamon, cardamom, and nutmeg, and a delightful sweetness that is somewhere between the taste offered by Maktoom and Barhi dates.
Although best enjoyed when simply eaten out of hand as a delicious snack, Amir dates are also ideal for a range of culinary applications. Given their soft nature, they are perfect for pureeing, but we'd especially recommend taking advantage of their immense sweetness by using them as a natural sweetener by chopping and sprinkling date pieces into smoothies, cereals, and baked goods recipes. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration!
As well as being extremely delectable and versatile, Amir dates also boast many nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre, and they contain good amounts of iron, potassium, and numerous antioxidants.

NAME: Dates - barhi
Description:
Barhi dates are smaller and more spherical than other date varieties. They have a lower-than-average astringency, meaning that they are edible during all three stages of ripeness. These dates are often still attached to the vine when sold in their unripe, yellow stage. The yellow Barhi date has a golden matte finish and a crunchy apple-like texture with a slight sweetness and mild astringency. If left at room temperature, it will eventually turn a brownish color as it ripens, becoming soft and chewy with a thin crisp outer skin.
They provide a varying degree of sweetness depending upon their ripeness level, ranging from fresh sugar cane to coconut and butterscotch - once fully ripe, Barhi dates are considered the sweetest and creamiest of all dates!
Although best enjoyed when simply eaten out of hand, Barhi dates are also ideal for a number of culinary applications, especially as they mature into softer, sweeter fruits. Once they reach this creamy sweetness, they are perfect for pureeing or using as a natural sweetener by chopping them and adding them to smoothies, cereals, and baked goods recipes. Their rich butterscotch flavour means they are particularly popular as ingredients in cake and sweet treat recipes! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration!
As well as being delicious and versatile, Barhi dates boast a number of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre and are rich in potassium.

NAME: Dates - medjool (Egypt)
Description:
Our 100% pure, organic Medjool dates from Egypt are a must-try!
The Medjool date is believed to be one of the worlds oldest cultivated fruits, with cultivation dating (pardon the pun) as far back as 4000 BC! They have been extremely popular in the Middle East and North Africa for thousands of years - the Ancient Egyptians are known to have used them to make an early form of wine!
Medjool dates are plump and oval in shape and slightly larger in size than other date varieties. They have wrinkled, glossy - their natural sugar crystals give rise to a distinctive shimmer - dark brown skin, underneath which is chewy, juicy, amber-coloured flesh that wows the tastebuds with its sweetness and undertones of caramel, honey, and cinnamon. Within the meaty flesh is a single elongated pit, which you need to remove before consumption.
Thanks to their succulence, softness - they have a softer texture than other dates - intense natural sweetness, and richly aromatic flavour, there are very few date varieties that can compare to the Medjool. Indeed, they are often called the Cadillac of Dates and the "King of Dates" due to their superior taste, size, and consistency!
Our Egyptian dates are some of the best quality Medjool dates you can buy. They are class 1 medium-sized fruits, 100% pure, and containing nothing but fruity goodness
Dates are perfect for snacking as well as a range of culinary uses! Although most commonly eaten fresh out of hand, they are also an ideal natural sweetener and sugar alternative. They are often chopped into pasta or rice dishes, and their sweetness makes them perfect for complementing savoury notes in vegetable and meat dishes, like lamb, pork, or poultry. You can blend dates into smoothies, press them into a syrup, or use them in baked goods like cakes, pies, and bread. We would particularly recommend making maamoul, scrumptious Middle Eastern cookies filled with date pudding that melt in the mouth! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes!

NAME: Durian
Description:
Regarded by many people in Southeast Asia as the "king of fruits", durian is distinctive for its strong odour, and formidable thorn-covered husk. The fruit can grow as large as 30 centimetres long and weighs up to 5kg.
The flavour is unique - compared to custard, almond, onion and vanilla!
Its shape ranges from oblong to round, the colour of its husk green to brown, and its flesh white to red.
Some people regard the durian as having a pleasantly sweet fragrance; others find the aroma overpowering with an unpleasant odour. The smell evokes reactions from deep appreciation to intense disgust but the supremely delectable flesh makes it worth the interesting aroma!
Durio zibethinus is the only species available in the international market: all other species are sold only in their local regions. There are hundreds of durian cultivars; many consumers express preferences for specific cultivars, which fetch higher prices in the market.
The durian, native to Southeast Asia, has been known to the Western world for about 600 years. The nineteenth-century British naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace described its flesh as "a rich custard highly flavoured with almonds". The flesh can be consumed at various stages of ripeness, and it is used to flavour a wide variety of savoury and sweet dishes in Southeast Asian cuisines. The seeds can also be eaten once cooked.

NAME: Durian - musang king
Description:
Durian fanatics usually regard musang king as one of the best durian varieties. It's known for the buttery, thick and creamy bright yellow flesh and rich flavour, with some bitterness to balance the sweetness.
The Malaysian durian musang king was originally known as 'raja kunyit'. This translates to 'turmeric king' which alludes to the colur of the deep-yellow flesh.
Musang king first established its reputation in the 80s when Tan Lai Fook from Raub, Pahang, Malaysia discovered a raja kunyit durian tree in Gua Musang, Kelantan. After bringing a branch of the tree back to Raub, this new breed started to attract other durian cultivators in the area.
The resulting durian cultivar was named after Gua Musang where it originated. In Chinese this durian is literally named "Cat Mountain King". This is either a phonetic rendering of musang or reference to the Malay meaning, the cat-like Asian palm civet.
The husk is dusky green-brown and usually features a distinctive star shape at the bottom.

NAME: Egg fruit
Description:
With a divine texture and flavour and believed to have been consumed by the Aztecs and Mayans, egg fruits are an absolute must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
Egg fruits are small to medium in size and have a round to oblong shape, sometimes bearing a tapered end. They have delicate, smooth, waxy skin that ripens from green to an eye-catching golden-yellow (and which often bears small brown patches).
Beneath their thin skin is bright yellow to orange-coloured flesh that delights eaters with its unique texture: egg fruit gets its name from the fact that its smooth, creamy, crumbly flesh has a similar texture to that of a hard-boiled egg yolk! The best varieties of egg fruit have a melt-in-the-mouth, mousse-like texture. The flesh may contain 1-6 large brown seeds.
Their flavour is equally dazzling. The rich, sweet flesh wows the tastebuds with its notes of sweet potato, pumpkin, and maple syrup!
As well as making them mouthwateringly delectable to eat fresh out of hand, this heavenly flavour profile makes egg fruits perfect for combining in an array of dessert recipes! As well as crumbling the soft flesh over salads, spreading it on toast, and dipping it in chocolate, it is ideal for baking and simmering and is popularly mixed with almond milk or soy milk to make a shake-like beverage.
During the Christmas season, egg fruits are popularly blended with milk, nutmeg, cinnamon, and vanilla to make vegan eggnog! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including scrumptious egg fruit ice cream!
Alongside being delicious and versatile, egg fruits boast numerous nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of beta-carotene, a pigment found within the flesh that is converted into vitamin A in the body, and are rich in calcium and phosphorus.

NAME: 'Fat pork' fruit
Description:
We bet even our most knowledgeable exotic fruit connoisseurs have never heard of 'fat pork' fruit!
This uniquely named specimen is the fruit of the chrysobalanus icaco tree, also known as the cocoplum or paradise plum tree, which is native to parts of Africa, the Americas, and the Caribbean. In Guyana, they are also known as 'fat poke'.
These very small fruits please the eye with their plump, round shape and their dazzling deep pink skin. Beneath this aesthetically pleasing, thin, smooth skin is divinely juicy white flesh that is spongy and has a largely neutral flavour with subtle notes of both tanginess and sweetness. Within the flesh is a central white seed - bite into it and it should split into two halves with a white interior that makes it resemble the interior of a coconut! This inner white coating can be eaten.
Although they are most commonly eaten fresh out of hand, since their soft, succulent flesh and bite-size nature means they make the perfect refreshing snack, they are also ideal for use in a number of recipes. We'd particularly recommend using them to make fruity jams and jellies, roasting the seeds for a uniquely appetizing morsel, and grounding the kernels of the seeds into a powder known as gbafilo or itsekiri, a favourable addition to West African soups. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some further inspiration!
As well as being delectable and culinarily versatile, fat pork fruit boasts a range of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin A and also provide a good amount of vitamins C and K.

NAME: Feijoa
Description:
The feijoa takes its name from the Portuguese botanist, Dom da Silva Feijoa, who discovered the fruit in Brazil. They are a distant member of the guava family - this is evident through the fruits' similar taste and aroma.
They can be up to the size of a small egg, however they are usually smaller than this and have tough dark green skin. The outer part of the flesh is grainy and firm but the central portion of the fruit is a sweet and creamy, clear jelly-like pulp.
The sweet aromatic flavour of this fruit is comparable to pineapple and guava, hence the nickname 'pineapple guava'.
The tiny edible seeds in the centre are not noticeable.
Feijoa are rich in Iodine and a great source of vitamin C.

Description:
One of the most eye-catching fruits that we sell, gac fruit is an absolute must-try for lovers of unusual fruits!

Although gac fruit is native to various regions in Southeast Asia, it has found particularly popularity in Vietnam. In fact, not only is the name 'gac' derived from the Vietnamese word for 'round', but in Vietnam, gac fruit is nicknamed the 'heavenly fruit' due to both its upward climbing nature (the vines can grow up to 6 metres tall!) and impressive nutritional benefits.

Gac fruits are small to medium in size and round to oblong in shape. Their skin, which ripens from green to yellow and finally to dark orange, has a leathery texture and is covered in hundreds of small spikes. Immediately beneath the distinctive skin is a layer of creamy orange flesh, enveloping a central core. Within this core are multiple seeds, encased in sticky red membranes - these soft, melt-in-the-mouth membranes are the edible parts of the fruit. 

These fruits are unique in that they can only be harvested when they are ripe. Therefore, although they have a hard texture when picked, they quickly turn soft. This is why we have choose to freeze some of our gac fruits: frozen fruits will last much longer than their fresh counterparts!

As the flesh has only a mild vegetal flavour (with notes of carrot, avocado, and tomato), gac fruit is usually cooked or juiced rather than consumed raw. We'd particularly recommend cooking the flesh as this maximises the flavour. The most common dish it's used for is sticky rice, particularly Xôi Gc in Vietnam.

NAME: Garlic - black garlic
Description:
Looking for a new way to add a kick of flavour to your mealtimes? Black garlic is just the thing for you!
Black garlic is the result of the fermentation of regular white garlic: fermented to perfection, the result is rich, sweet, visually stunning black cloves.

With both sweet and savoury notes, black garlic infuses dishes with a perfect mix of molasses-like richness and tangy garlic undertones - we particularly noted hints of balsamic vinegar and, intriguingly, tamarind! It has a tender, smooth texture with a melt-in-your-mouth consistency similar to a soft dried fruit.
Its umami flavour makes black garlic the perfect addition to a number of dishes, adding a punch of garlic taste to your mains, sides, and even sweet treats! We recommend using the cloves the way you would use roasted garlic: purée them with oil, then smear the paste on crostini, incorporate it into dressings, or rub it onto chicken or fish before roasting. If you ground the garlic to a powder, you have the perfect condiment to sprinkle on anything that needs some earthiness and depth. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipes!
As well as having culinary versatility, black garlic also boasts many nutritional benefits. In particular, it is rich in many antioxidants - black garlic contains substantially more antioxidants than regular garlic! - and is believed to reduce the body's 'bad' cholesterol and boost immunity.

NAME: Giving Back - Philippines 2017
Description:
Since we established in 2014, we've made 11 business trips to Asia. Each time, we have directly encountered thousands of people who are living in very difficult circumstances, almost unimaginable to many people living in the western world. Some of these people have little or no access to official government support.
As our business continues to grow, we want to do all we can to help by giving something back to the people who need it.
As a result, twice each year, the staff at My Exotic Fruit visit a country in Asia to give back our time and money to local charities, and directly to the people, where appropriate.
This does mean we have to close our business, but we hope you can understand, this is something which is very close to our hearts.
Our next 'giving back' trip is confirmed to be
Giving Back
In 2013, when we started this project, we decided the most appropriate way for us to 'give back' was to distribute fresh fruit to local charities and the local people in need.
The process is simple, we buy fresh fruit, always from the local vendors, and spend a few days working with local charities to pass the fruit on to those who are in need. People who are unable to work, or only earn a few dollars per day, and struggle to afford nutritious food for their families. We have heard stories of the poorest people bulking out their meals with non-food ingredients as they are cheaper.
We gladly pay for this out of our profits, and will continue to do so, but before previous trips to Asia, some of our customers asked how they can get involved. This is great as it will help us distribute even more fruit to the charities.
We have created this option in our online shop and are offering our customers the opportunity to donate as little as £1 towards this good cause by adding this to your basket when ordering. If you are able to donate more, please simply increase the quantity.
We completely understand that many of you may prefer to contribute directly and individually rather than via a business. This opportunity to donate is entirely optional.
We thank you sincerely, in advance, for your support of our giving back mission.
You can follow our progress on social media.

NAME: Golden apple (june plum)
Description:
Mature golden apple are roughly the size of an egg.
Whilst green, they have crunchy flesh which is a little sour. Once they've ripened and turned yellow, the juicy golden flesh has a pineapple-mango aroma and flavour. They're sweet, with a hint of acidity.
It's common for the skin of golden apples to be rough and blemished.
In many parts of the world, the green fruit are used in raw salads like som tam in Thailand and rojak in Malaysia and also eaten as a snack, after being dipped into fish sauce, salt or shrimp paste.
Golden apple juice, which can be made from green or yellow fruits, is popular in the Caribbean and Southeast Asia. It's mixed with water, and sugar or salt to taste. Sometimes dried sour or salted plums are added to the juice.
The leaves of the golden apple tree are used as seasoning and in salads.
Golden apple from the Caribbean are larger and will usually ripen to a sweet flavour and golden yellow colour. They can be eaten fresh out of hand or used to make sweeter juice.
The golden apple from Asia are smaller, harvested when very young and unripe. They can be used for pickling, adding to salads and to make sour juice but they won't usually ripen.

Yamanshi sits at the heart of Japans reputation for world-renowned fruit cultivation. As the peach capital, Yamanshi is the perfect environment for growing high sugar low acid peaches, and there is no peach more delicious than the Hakuto.

Beneath their delicate skin is a fine-textured, juicy and deliciously aromatic flesh with a high sugar content, typically ranging from 12 to 14 on the Brix scale and ideal for those who prefer sweet fruits.
Each peach is meticulously hand-grown in controlled conditions. They are convered with small paper bags while they are green to encourage them to grow pale and sweet. Harvesting is a delicate process, plucked by hand.
During summer gift-giving season, chugen, these peaches are a prized gift to give loved ones or important clients.

Description:
Hala fruit is a little-known gem.
Cultivated in various regions around the world, primarily Southeast Asia, the Pacific Islands, Hawaii, and Australia, this large fruit - it can grow up to 30cm long! - dazzles people first and foremost with their truly unique appearance. Made up of a central white stone surrounded by multiple (from dozens to hundreds) green-tipped red segments, called 'keys', that resemble pieces of quartz, hala fruits look almost otherworldly - indeed, many people say they look like exploding planets!
The delightful floral aroma is matched by a similarly brilliant taste. Beneath the inedible skin of the keys is a thick pulp that has a sweet, delicate, tropical flavour, with some comparing it to mango and pineapple, noting undertones of banana, whilst others say the taste is comparable to sugarcane; the very fibrous green tips of the keys are edible too, and even the central seed can be eaten, although it is usually roasted first. As well as eating it raw, hala fruits are also commonly boiled, baked, and dried to make a paste that closely resembles dates in both appearance and flavour; the flesh can be boiled with sugar and made into a delicious jam, and refreshing juice can be extracted from the fruit.
Hala fruits are a great source of dietary fibre, and contain high amounts of beneficial vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants.

NAME: Ice cream bean
Description:
Ice cream beans are one of the most unique items that we sell!
These fruits originating from Latin America consist of cylindrical pods that vary considerably in size, measuring anywhere from 50 to 100cm in length. These curved pods have leathery, semi-thick green skin that becomes yellowish-brown when the fruits are fully ripe. Beneath this textured skin is fluffy white flesh encasing numerous seeds. The flesh is simply delightful: in texture, it is pulpy, spongy, and delicate - almost resembling candyfloss, and to the touch it is reminiscent of cotton wool! - and its taste is similarly enchanting, combining notes of vanilla, cream, and cinnamon!
This intensely sweet flesh is best enjoyed when simply scooped out of the pods. Indeed, in Latin America, the moist flesh is consumed raw as a refreshing sweet snack to quench people's thirst! However, the pulp also has a variety of culinary applications: they are perfect for adding gentle sweetness to salads, smoothies, and cocktails (and mocktails)! The flesh is used in its raw form as it is not able to withstand the heat from cooking.
As well as being delicious, ice cream beans boast numerous nutritional benefits. In particular, they are rich in calcium, dietary fibre, and vitamin C. The pods/outer skins of ice cream beans are inedible. The seeds of the fruit are edible only when cooked; do not eat them raw.

NAME: Jalapeño green, orange and purple - fresh and frozen
Description:
Jalapeños are perfect for adding a kick of heat to your mealtimes!
Originally hailing from Mexico - they got the name jalapeño from Xalapa, the capital of the Mexican state of Veracruz - but now cultivated around the world, jalapeños are members of the nightshade family, alongside potatoes and tomatoes, but they are more commonly known as the chilli peppers that are used to flavour salsa and salad dressing.
Green when harvested, jalapeños turn red as they ripen, although they are usually used in an unripened state. Yet green and red jalapeños are not all the varieties you can try - eye-catching orange and purple jalapeños are a must-try! Crunchy in texture, jalapeños have a fresh flavour that is similar to that of a green bell pepper, and are renowned for their spiciness. The heat varies from pepper to pepper - purple jalapeños are milder and sweeter than green peppers; orange peppers are the sweetest and juiciest - but they are mild enough to be eaten whole.
Jalapeños can be enjoyed in many different ways: you can dice or mince them to spread the heat throughout a salad dressing or salsa; add slices of jalapeño to nachos and tacos if you fancy an intensely tangy bite, or fill them with cheese, cover with breadcrumbs, and deep-fry them to recreate a popular American snack! You can also dry and smoke jalapeños to turn them into chipotles, and they are additionally ideal for pickling if you want to try a new, delicious condiment to serve alongside your favourite meals. We recommend making spicy jalapeño poppers, a delectable appetizer perfect for a dinner party, and a refreshing, super healthy Mexican corn salad! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for the recipes.
For those who enjoy a more moderate flavour, we suggest removing the jalapeño's seeds and ribs, but remember to wash your hands straight after doing so as their oils might cause discomfort if they come into contact with your eyes, nose, and sensitive areas of skin.
As well as being very flavoursome, jalapeños are also nutritionally valuable, being a good source of dietary fibre and boasting a high content of various vitamins (namely vitamins A and B6) and minerals. Purple jalapeños in particular are renowned for their high vitamin C content.

NAME: Japanese persimmon (luxury fruit for gifting)
Description:
Experience the taste of autumn in Japan with Fuyu persimmon.
Widely regarded as a traditional autumn treat (persimmon is the national fruit of Japan!), Fuyu persimmon is an ancient delicacy. Of the 1000 varieties in Japan, Fuyu stands out as one of the most popular persimmons in the world.
Beneath glossy orange and satisfyingly crisp skin is a melt-in-the-mouth sweet flesh that will keep you hooked. Their taste is very sweet with hints of cinnamon, honey and brown sugar.
They are non astringent and offer different flavours at different stages of ripeness. As the fruit ripens, it becomes softer and juicier with a gloriously intensified sweetness.
Our black sesame persimmons are just as sweet and juicy, while being even more unique. An uncommon black-flesh variety, these persimmons get their colour from a specific growing method. The fruits are exposed to sunlight for a longer period of time and picked only when completely mature, creating a deeper sweetness and a non-astringent texture.
Although best enjoyed simply eaten fresh out of hand, Japanese persimmons are very versatile, being suited to a range of culinary applications whether they are firm and dense or have the softness and squishiness of full maturity. We'd especially recommend cooking them into jams and chutneys, adding slices to fruit salads, chopping them into salsas, and incorporating them into sweet baked goods such as tarts and pies!
As well as being versatile, Japanese persimmons are a good source of vitamin A and C, as well as dietary fibre and antioxidants.

Description:
Jocote fruit, pronounced ho-CO-tay, and also known by many other names, grow on deciduous trees in warm tropical climates. They grow on thick irregular branches in clusters, or alone. Unusually, the fruits begin to develop following tiny red flowers before the leaves appear.
The small tantalising fruits which are often unevenly shaped, have a sweet plum-like flavour and soft juicy golden yellow flesh which melts in the mouth. The shiny and waxy red skin is edible however the large central seed is to be discarded.
Young jocote fruits usually ripen from green-yellow to a purple or red colour although some variants of the species will ripen to a yellow color. We also sell yellow jocote, click here to find out more.
Jocote fruit are rich in vitamin C and carbohydrates. They are a source of calcium, phosphorus, iron and a small amount of fibre. They contain carotene, B-complex vitamins, and several important amino acids. Jocotes are high in antioxidants, which help rid the body of free radicals.

Description:
Are you a tea lover looking for a new herbal blend? Then we have just the thing for you!
Kinkeliba (also called kinkiliba), a plant native to West Africa, has been used for centuries for both culinary and medicinal purposes. The leaves of the kinkeliba shrub were traditionally, and still are today, used to make a healthy, caffeine-free, herbal tea. There are regional variations in consumption of the tea, with those in Mali and Senegal traditionally drinking the beverage at breakfast, whereas in other areas the leaves are combined with sugar and milk and is drunk with bread at sundown as a way of breaking the daily fast. Indeed, it is considered particularly perfect for this purpose due to the tea's sweet flavour and the belief that it is an appetite stimulant - those who have been fasting want to be able to enjoy as much rich food as possible in the evening after eating nothing from sunrise to sunset.
However, with its pleasant woody flavour and exceptional, slightly lemony aroma, kinkeliba tea is ideal for drinking at any time of any day! When mixed with mint, lemon, ginger, and cloves, we're sure this uniquely flavoured tea will delight your tastebuds!
As well as being delectable, kinkeliba tea boasts many nutritional benefits: as well as boasting antioxidant properties, it is believed to aid digestion and have anti-ageing benefits.

Ripe kiwano has orange skin and lime green, jelly-like flesh with a refreshingly fruity taste, and texture similar to a passionfruit or pomegranate. The flavour is intriguingly compared to a unique combination of cucumber, banana and lemon/lime!
Kiwano is a traditional food plant in Africa. Along with the Gemsbok cucumber, and Tsamma (Citron melon) it is one of the few sources of water during the dry season in the Kalahari Desert. In northern Zimbabwe it is called gaka or gakachika, and is primarily used as a snack or salad, and rarely for decoration. It can be eaten at any stage of ripening, but when overripened, will burst forcefully to release seeds.
Some people also eat the peel, which is very rich in vitamin C and dietary fibre.
Health benefits include high in vitamin A, beta carotene and magnesium.

NAME: Kola nut
Description:
Love Coca-Cola? Then we have just the thing for you: kola nuts.
Kola nuts are small brown nuts (roughly the same size as chestnuts) found inside the star-shaped fruits that grow on kola trees, a species of tree native to West Africa.
Each nut is packed with caffeine, so when they are eaten fresh they have a somewhat bitter taste. However, dried kola nuts have a much milder flavour and boast a delightful aroma comparable to nutmeg.
Kola nuts are prized in West Africa for their stimulant effects: one nut contains more caffeine than two cups of coffee, so it's not surprising that it is common for people to chew the nuts to get their daily caffeine kick! So well known did the powerful effects of kola nuts become that in the 19th century kola extract was used in a variety of purportedly energy boosting medicines, and by the 20th-century the inventors of Coca-Cola added the extract to their recipe - indeed, the 'cola' in the brand's name is derived from 'kola'!
Although kola nut extract is apparently no longer in Coca-Cola, it is still used in many popular energy drinks, so you have probably experienced the kola nut without realising it!

Looking for a new way to add some subtle citrus flavour to your mealtimes? Lemongrass is just the thing for you!
Although it is not very well-known in the UK, lemongrass - a tall, perennial grass native to Sri Lanka and India - is extremely popular throughout Asia, so much so that the herb is regarded as one of the staples of South Asian (particularly Thai) cuisine.
This popularity is unsurprising given the wonderful flavour of lemongrass. As its name suggests, lemongrass has not only an aroma reminiscent of lemon, but its citrus flavour is similar to lemons too (with glorious undertones of ginger). In fact, lemongrass actually possesses the same oils as lemons and is often used as a substitute for tangy lemon flavouring!
Its fresh, floral, and almost minty aroma, combined with its zesty taste, means lemongrass works well in both sweet and savoury dishes, complimenting everything from your favourite baked goods to steaks! They are also ideal for making drinks, with lemongrass becoming a common choice among distillers - the herb is appearing in spirits, beers, sports drinks, and herbal teas.
We'd particularly recommend using the versatile herb to infuse some vibrant lemon flavour into your curries and soups, and making sublime sauces and marinades. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including iced tea, shrimp and lemongrass skewers, and a vanilla and lemongrass creme brulee that will wow your dinner party guests!
As well as being delicious, lemongrass boasts many nutritional benefits. Used for centuries in Ayurvedic (Indian) medicine, lemongrass is still valued today for its richness of vitamins and minerals, notably vitamins A and C, folate, and niacin.

Description:
One of our rarest fruits, lucuma is a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
Lucuma is native to South America and it has a much-celebrated history in the region. It was hailed by the Incas as the tree of life and they even held festivals in the fruit's honour; today, lucuma is a national fruit of Chile and at least 26 villages in Peru are named after the fruit!
It is small to medium in size and round to oval in shape, somewhat reminiscent of avocadoes at first glance. Beneath its smooth, thin, dark green skin is golden-orange flesh that is sure to delight your tastebuds! The starchy, dry flesh is often closely compared to cooked egg yolk in texture, but its fantastic savour is much harder to describe: we'd say the flesh combines the flavours of maple syrup, sweet potato, and butterscotch!
The sublime sugary flavour of lucuma's flesh makes the fruit perfect for eating fresh out of hand (although the skin and seeds are discarded). However, the fruit is extremely versatile, perfect for use in any number of recipes! The flesh is commonly dried and ground into a powder which has become a popular sugar substitute. With a taste similar to brown sugar, lucuma powder is an ideal flavouring to use in your favourite baked goods recipes, and also imparts brilliant sweetness to yoghurt, cereal, and oatmeal. In Peru, lucuma powder is additionally utilised to flavour ice cream and is often blended with milk or fruit juice to make smoothies. Lucuma can be cooked too - we'd particularly recommend simmering them into jams, syrups, and preserves! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration!
As well as being wonderfully delectable, lucumas are nutritionally beneficial. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre and provide a good amount of vitamin C.
Our frozen lucuma is just as delicious and nutritious as their fresh counterparts. Made of 100% pure fruit, all of our frozen lucuma options - frozen lucuma halves, pulp, and whole fruits - provide much of the sweetness of fresh lucuma and, once fully defrosted, can be enjoyed in many of the same ways! We'd particularly recommend using the frozen flesh to make excellent lucuma milkshakes.
