Lulo are a must-try for all exotic fruit lovers!
Small in size and round in shape, in appearance, lulo somewhat resemble small oranges. Indeed, lulo are also known as 'naranjilla', the Spanish term for 'little orange'. Their thick orange skin is delicate (these fruits are easily bruised), smooth, and leathery to the touch.
Yet, whilst on the outside lulo look like oranges, on the inside, they bear a resemblance to tomatoes. The green, jelly-like flesh is separated into 4 sections and has small, pale yellow seeds. The flesh has a rich aroma, with distinctly sour notes and a flavour that delights the tastebuds: it has a notably citrus taste, sometimes described as a spectacular combination of rhubarb, pineapple, kiwi and lime!
The fruits are best enjoyed when eaten fresh out of hand: simply cut the lulo in half, add some salt, squeeze out the pulp and discard the rinds, then devour! However, their sweet-sour taste means they are also ideal for a range of culinary applications. They are commonly used to make refreshing juice and delectable jams, jellies, and sauces. You can use lulo pulp as a filling in baked goods and to make delicious lulo ice cream, sherbet, or sorbet, each of which is perfect for anyone with a sweet tooth! The pulp even works well in savoury meat stews! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including a quick recipe for the brilliant Colombian drink 'lulada', which is made from the fruit's green juice.
As well as being supremely delectable, lulo boasts numerous nutritional benefits. In particular, they are a good source of dietary fibre and vitamins C, A, and K.
Our frozen lulo pulp is the flesh of ripe lulo fruits frozen in a container or vacuum bag. Made of 100% pure fruit, the pulp offers much of the same brilliant citrus flavour and, once fully defrosted, can be used in many of the same ways as fresh lulo. One of the most popular uses of frozen lulo pulp is to simply mix it with water or milk to make healthy, refreshing juice - our 500g sachets make up to 1.5L of juice!

NAME: Lychee
Description:
Lychee are a must-try for all exotic fruit lovers!
These fruits native to China are small in size and round to oval in shape. They have thin, bumpy skin that delights the sight with its appealing reddish-pink hue (although some varieties are still green in colour even when fully mature).
Beneath the easily peelable skin of these plump, delightfully aromatic fruits is glistening translucent to opaque white flesh that has a delectably sweet, floral flavour, with musky, citrus undertones. We've noted hints of rose water, watermelon, strawberry, and melon, making each bite of these fruits a real taste sensation! The thick, juicy flesh is somewhat firm, and has a slight, soft crunch - the texture can be compared to that of a chewy, crisp grape. The flesh easily detaches from the medium/large, dark brown central seed which is inedible. We'd particularly recommend our new 'kway may pink' (also known as 'kwai mai pink') variety of lychee. Although these Chinese lychee are harvested later in the season than other types, they still have the spiked, reddish-pink shell and the delicious, sweet and juicy flesh that lychee are known for.
To best enjoy their amazing aroma (with notes of sweet fruits and roses) and flavour, simply consume them fresh out of hand, making sure to remove the skin and seed. However, they are well-suited to a number of culinary applications. They are commonly mixed into green and fruit salads and taste sublime when halved and served over desserts, ice cream, or shaved ice, or incorporated in recipes for puddings, custards, crumbles, cupcakes, and cakes. Lychees can additionally be simmered into sauces and spooned over seafood dishes, cooked into jams, or infused into syrups. Why not follow Haitian custom by stuffing lychees with cream cheese and topping them with macadamia nuts? Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including a nectarine and lychee cobbler!
As well as being delicious, lychee have been used in traditional Chinese medicine for centuries, and still today are valued for boasting many nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and provide good amounts of potassium, dietary fibre, copper, and B vitamins.

Description:
Looking for an unusual way to add some tropical flavour to your diet? Our madd fruit in jars is just the thing for you!
Madd fruit grows on vines in the African savannahs and takes over a year to become ready to harvest. They are picked after the first rains of the season, in April and May. The orange to brown-coloured fruit has a hard, spherical shell that contains seeds which are coated with a soft and juicy yellow pulp. The flavour is simultaneously tart and sweet.
In Africa, madd fruit is easy to find in street markets, where it's sold topped with sugar and/or salt and pepper. It can also be eaten neat but most people prefer to season the pulp. Mixed with water and sugar, the pulp makes a delicious juice. It's not advisable to swallow the seeds but the inside of the shell is covered with pulp that can be consumed.
Madd fruit is rich in vitamin C and also contains vitamin B6, calcium, phosphorus and magnesium.
In the region of Casamance in Senegal, bunches of roots from the madd plant are sometimes strung outside homes to protect the inhabitants from evil spirits.
This product is made by Zena Exotic Fruits, which is a family-owned, eco-friendly company based in Dakar, Senegal in West Africa. Zena supports non-profit organisations that help young children's education in Senegal. By purchasing Zena products, you are supporting Africa.

Mamey is round or slightly irregular, with a brown or grey-brown rind that is a few milimetres thick.
Mamey usually range from 10-15cm in diameter.

Small fruits contain a single seed, while larger ones might have up to four.

Description:

Black mangoes (also known as 'blackie mangoes') are a favourite fruit in their native Jamaica, and for good reason!
Although, like other mangoes, black mangoes have a round to oblong shape and a small to medium size, they vary in the colour of their peel. Despite their name, neither their skin nor their flesh is black in colour - they are called black mangoes to distinguish them from mangoes that turn red upon maturing, since the skin of black mangoes instead remains yellowish-green in colour even when fully ripe.
Beneath their smooth, delicate, aesthetically appealing skin is eye-catching, tender orange pulp that emits a spectacular floral fragrance and is sure to wow your tastebuds with its divine sweetness and mouthwatering succulence. As well as being supremely aromatic, refreshing, and delectable, black mangoes are almost entirely fibreless, meaning that they are an easier - and infinitely less messy! - fruit to enjoy.
Although they are best enjoyed when simply eaten fresh out of hand, black mangoes are also a superior culinary ingredient. Whilst their sweetness makes them perfect for dessert recipes, they are very versatile and therefore can be used in a range of savoury applications too! We'd particularly recommend using them to make delicious jams and chutneys, blending them into smoothies, capitalising on their rich tropical savour to liven up your cocktails (and mocktails!), and stirring some into curries to balance out their spiciness. As well as being brilliantly appetizing, black mangoes boast a range of nutritional benefits too. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre, have a high content of vitamins A and C, and include a good amount of magnesium and potassium.

Description:

This succulent texture and satisfying sweetness mean Irwin mangoes are best eaten fresh out of hand. However, they are also ideal for a variety of food and drink recipes, from smoothies and sorbets to cakes and tarts. As they are also known as 'apple mangoes' due to the fact they have a similar flavour to the classic fruit, they are particularly well suited as an apple substitute in a plethora of sweet recipes, perfect for when you want to put an exotic spin on a traditional recipe!
Like other mangoes, Irwin mangoes are great sources of vitamin C and dietary fibre, and also contain enzymes that are beneficial for digestion.

Beneath their bright skin is a vivid golden yellow flesh that is intensely sweet, supremely juicy, and almost entirely fibreless. Their creamy texture means that each bite practically melts in the mouth.
Its not hard to see why Miyasaki mangoes are so delicious, when you discover how much time, effort and expertise goes into their cultivation. Grown exclusively in Miyasaki, southern Japan, these special mangoes are kept inside temperature-controlled greenhouses where everything from humidity to sunlight are controlled at every stage.
Farmers are so precise that up to 80% of young mango buds are removed from each tree, allowing the remaining fruit to receive the full benefit of nutrients and ensuring that they can grow larger and sweeter.
Each fruit is wrapped in a protective net above a strategically placed reflector to ensure the sun hits evenly. Farmers then wait for the fruit to naturally fall from the tree, a sign that they are perfectly ripe. Even then, each fruit is rigorously tested for weight, sugar content, shape and appearance, meaning that only the best are chosen.
Such efforts mean you can be assured that each Miyasaki mango you receive is the best it could possibly be, offering an unrivalled taste experience.

Description:
Mangosteen are without a doubt one of the most exquisite fruits of the tropics - you're missing out if you don't try some!
In the late 19th century, it was rumoured Queen Victoria would grant a knighthood to anyone who brought her mangosteen. This, as well as its superb flavour, was enough to earn the mangosteen a new name, "the queen of fruits".
Still today, these small purple-skinned fruits are very highly regarded, and for good reason. Beneath their hard skin is fibrous, white, segmented flesh that is refreshingly juicy and has a delightful flavour: one bite of mangosteen's delicate flesh will dazzle your tongue with a distinctive combination of both sweet and citrus notes, and the succulent flesh will create an explosion of flavours in your mouth. We'd say the taste is most comparable to a mouthwatering mix of lychee, peach, grape and pineapple, although some people liken mangosteen to sherbet!
Mangosteen are most often eaten fresh out of hand, but they are also ideal for use in a variety of food and drink recipes. We'd particularly recommend using them to make scrumptious jams (perfect for adding some exotic flavour to your toast!), blending them to create creamy smoothies, and serving them with ice cream, a spectacularly flavoursome dessert. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite mangosteen recipes, including a heavenly panna cotta!
As well as being delicious, mangosteen also boast a myriad of nutritional benefits. For instance, they are an excellent source of fibre, are rich in vitamins C and B9, and contain many beneficial anti-oxidants, including xanthones, a unique plant compound believed to have strong antioxidant properties.

NAME: Medlar
Description:
Cultivated since the Roman period, medlars' delicious flavour makes them a popular choice among fruit lovers even today!
Medlar are a small fruit that looks like a cross-between of a small apple and a rosehip. When ripe and ready to harvest, medlar are hard and acidic, but become edible after being 'bletted'. Bletting is a process whereby the fruits soften through exposure to frost or being kept in cold storage. The process can take a long time but the delicious taste makes them worth the wait!
Once softening begins, the skin rapidly takes on a wrinkled texture and turns dark brown. As such, a softened fruit can look as if it has spoiled, but don't worry, this actually means that they are at the perfect stage for consumption! Once fully ripe, the flesh gains an almost liquid consistency and has a multi-layered flavour that is rich and complex: some people compare the sweet taste to dates, whilst others say the flavour is reminiscent of toffee apples or apple sauce. Either way, this unique flavour is sure to wow your tastebuds!
Although, once fully bletted, they are most often eaten raw - they are scrumptious with creme fraiche or yoghurt or as an accompaniment to cheese - medlars can be used for a variety of culinary applications. As medlars are high in pectin, they are ideal for making jelly, and it is also popular to turn these fruits into medlar cheese, a type of curd made with sugar, butter, and eggs.
As well as being delectable, medlars boast a range of nutritional benefits: they are rich in vitamins C and B and are a good source of protein, calcium, and iron.
Our frozen perfectly-ripe whole medlar fruits are just as healthy and delectable as the fresh fruit themselves, and they keep for up to a month in the freezer, so they are perfect for those who want their medlar to last for longer.

Description:
Charentais melons are a must-try for melon lovers!
Native to the south of France (specifically the fields surrounding the town of Cavaillon) but cultivated around the globe, charentais melons are small in size and round to oval in shape. They have eye-catching skin: the thin, wrinkled rind ranges in colour from grey-green to pale green, and displays distinctive dark green stripes.
They have a divine aroma, emitting a fragrance that stuns with its honeyed, fruity, and floral notes reminiscent of ambrosia. Their flavour is similarly sublime. Beneath the wonderful exterior is light orange flesh and a central cavity packed with oblong ivory seeds, attached to small white fibres. The flesh is supremely succulent and sweet, although the mild acidity of charentais melons means this sweetness is balanced out, with a notable floral aftertaste. Indeed, their heavenly flavour has made them so renowned in France that they are annually celebrated in the world-famous 'Feria du Melon a Cavaillon', the Melon Fair of Cavaillon, and charentais melons have earned more sufficient regarded to be hailed a speciality variety.
To best enjoy these brilliant fruits, simply remove the rind and seeds, and devour the flesh! However, charentais melons are also ideal for a range of culinary applications - their combination of fresh sweetness and faint sour notes makes them well-suited to savoury as well as sweet recipes. For example, it is popular to mix them into salads; wrap slices of melon in prosciutto; sprinkle thin pieces with salt and lime juice for an appetizing snack; serve them with fish or poultry, and use them to make sorbets. Why not respect their French roots by slicing or scooping the melons into bite-sized pieces and serving with a sweet wine or port? We'd also suggest pickling them so they can be enjoyed all year round! Check out our 'Further information' tab for some of our favourite recipes.
Alongside being refreshing and full of flavour, charentais melons also boast many nutritional benefits. They are rich in vitamin C and dietary fibre, are a good source of vitamins A and B, and provide potassium, zinc, and calcium.
For a snack-sized option, try our baby charentais melons which weigh between 420g and 620g.

NAME: Melon - orange watermelon
Description:
Love melons but growing tired of standard supermarket varieties? Our orange watermelons from Murcia (Spain) are just the thing for you!
Orange watermelons are thought to originate from Africa, where they have been cultivated for millennia - paintings dating to ancient Egyptian times show watermelons were highly regarded as a key water source! In fact, it's believed that yellow and orange watermelons were by far the most common varieties of the fruit in existence, with the red flesh melons being a rare mutation.
Given how red watermelons have spiked in popularity, orange watermelons are today a speciality item, only available from select fruit retailers. As such, our website is one of the few places you can buy this amazing fruit in the UK!
These melons are typically small to medium in size, on average weighing around 1.5kg to 2kg per fruit. They will feel heavy for their size - this indicates ripeness. Like other melons, orange watermelons are round or oblong in shape, however they do not display the typical distinct striping which we are used to seeing on the outer rind of watermelons. Instead, there is fine, deep green mottling dispersed sporadically over the lighter green backdrop. You may notice a yellow spot on your watermelon which is the underside, known as the belly. Once ready to harvest the spot turns from white to yellow.
The flesh is bright orange - perfect to bring a splash of colour to salads and desserts! If in season, why not add a yellow watermelon to your basket too - you could easily create a rainbow on your plates with just a few of our tropical fruits! The texture and flavour of the flesh are just as astounding as its appearance: the flesh has a divine crispness and will delight your tastebuds with its supreme juiciness, delicate sweetness, and glorious tropical notes.
Their subtle sweetness makes these fruits ideal for both sweet and savoury recipes. We'd especially recommend using them to make a spicy watermelon soup to bring a kick of heat to your mealtimes, some refreshing watermelon sorbet that will cool you down in the summer heat, and a scrumptious halloumi, watermelon, and mint salad! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for these recipes!
We receive both seeded and seedless orange watermelons from our suppliers across the season, aiming to source the seeded varieties as much as possible.
As well as boasting a mouthwatering taste, orange watermelons provide a range of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are a good source of vitamins A and C, and are rich in potassium, magnesium, and dietary fibre.

NAME: Melon - yubari king melon (luxury fruit for gifting)
Description:
Meet the worlds most luxury melon, the Yubari King melon.
As one of the most expensive fruits in Japan, the Yubari King melon is highly regarded and sought after. So much so, that each year their harvesting peak is celebrated at the Yubari melon festival with an auction. Theyre so renowned, that one year, a pair of Yubari king melons sold for an incredible 5 million yen! (Thats £25,000!).
It takes incredible patience and dedication to grow a Yubari king melon, as well as perfect conditions. Its so aligned with its environment that attempts to grow it elsewhere consistently fail to match the same extraordinary quality.
Their journey begins in the winter in heated greenhouses. In Spring, farmers lay mats underneath to help them grow into perfect spheres with just the right amount of sunlight. At harvest, Yubari king melons are rigorously inspected for sugar content, net pattern, shape and size and only the best are sold.
Such strict measures make for a melon with a extremely soft and juicy flesh, a strong tropical aroma and a wonderful sweetness. In fact, some people find the Yubari so sweet that they prefer to enjoy with a glass of water.
Such a premium melon makes for an extremely prestigious gift. In fact, they are frequently exchanged in Japan during formal ceremonies, celebrations or to express gratitude in a gesture of respect and goodwill.
They are a variety that ripen quicker than others. Therefore, it's exceptionally unsuual to see them outside of Japan.
Gift the Yubari king melon to someone truly special or indulge in the luxury yourself.

Monk fruit
Description:
Monk fruit is harvested in the form of a round, green fruit, which becomes brown on drying. It is rarely used in its fresh form, as it is hard to store.
Thus, the fruits are usually dried before further use and are sold in this fashion in Chinese herbal shops. The fruits are slowly dried in ovens, preserving them and removing most of the unwanted aromas.
The dried fruits are used in the preparation of teas, soups, and as a sweetener for products that would usually have sugar or honey added to them
Monk fruit, whose extract is nearly 300 times sweeter than sugar, has been used in China as a low-calorie sweetener for cooling drinks and in traditional Chinese medicine. We also have a broken shell option, this is just where the shell has split.

NAME: Noni (also known as vomit fruit!)
Description:
Noni is a tropical plant native to Polynesia. Not only does it look unusual, it also has a particualy unique flavour and aroma! These small rough-skinned fruits are very pale to honey-yellow in colour when ripe.
Most commonly compared to strong cheese, noni is more often consumed for its health benefits rather than its flavour.
Fresh ripe noni is certainly a fruit that any fruit lover would enjoy trying once but in countries where it grows, it has a regular place in the diet for many. It is eaten raw, with cheese and salt, which is believed to complement its savoury taste. It's sometimes also cooked and eaten with curry, and in Thailand, noni is added to some types of som-tam, a popular salad made with green papaya. Its leaves are used in Thai cuisine too.
Noni drink can be made by either blending the fruits with water or fermenting them. The fermented drink is usually consumed in small doses on a daily basis as a nutritional supplement.
Noni fruits are particularly difficult for us to source as there are few commerical farms, on which the majority of the harvest is used for drink production. Also, noni can ripen and become soft very quickly, making them a challenging fruit to successfully export. We have limited availability of this fruit so if you're eager to try, we would advise purchasing as soon as you see it in stock, as it's likely they wont last long!

NAME: Papaya (Brazil)
Description:
Papayas are mouthwatering and incredibly nutritious fruits that all exotic fruit lovers need to try!
Papayas are elongated to spherical shape and can be as long as 50cm (although the fruits we receive from our farmers are usually 20cm to 30cm in length). Their smooth, glossy skin is deep green in colour when the fruits are immature, however the skin develops orange-yellow hues as the fruits ripen.
Beneath their appealing skin is bright orange flesh encasing a cavity filled with many black seeds, each seed surrounded by a bubble of flavourless jelly. Both the flesh and seeds are edible! Once the papaya is fully ripe, the eye-catching flesh becomes so soft that it boasts a butter-like consistency, and this wonderfully creamy flesh wows with its combination of sweet notes - hints of mango, peach, and banana can be detected! - and distinctively musky undertones. The crunchy seeds contribute to the unique flavour profile of papaya, as they taste just like pepper!
As well as simply eating the flesh and seeds out of hand, papayas are also perfect for use in any number of sweet and savoury recipes! The spicy seeds can be added to salads and can be ground to create a substitute for peppercorns, whilst the flesh is ideal for making salsa, sorbet, smoothies, and more! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including no-churn papaya ice cream!
Alongside being divinely delectable, papayas are extremely healthy. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and dietary fibre, and are packed full of enzymes that aid digestion.

NAME: Passionfruit - curuba
Description:
A member of the passionfruit family, the curuba looks somewhat like a straight, small banana with rounded ends, hence the nickname 'banana passion fruit'. It's yellow to green once ripe and has an orange pulp (with several black seeds) which is often enjoyed with a little sugar.
The curuba is used to flavour meringues, cakes, fruit sauces and gelatin desserts such as 'esponjada de curuba'. Another popular treat in Colombia is curuba ice cream. Because of curubas high pectin content, it is also used to make fruit preserves. It can be used in fruit salads, crepes, yoghurt; in fact, anywhere that passionfruit is used! Our frozen curuba pulp is also ideal for making refreshing juice, the ideal thirst-quencher! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including a brilliant passionfruit and mango roulade!
Like passionfruit, curuba is a good source of dietary fibre, gained primarily from the seeds. The fruit is also high in phosphorous, niacin, calcium, iron and sodium. Curuba is high in vitamin C and contains vitamin A too.

NAME: Pear - deveci 'honey pear'
Description:
One of the most renowned pear varieties, deveci pears are an absolute must-try for fruit lovers!
Deveci pears hail from Turkey - combining the texture of an Asian pear with the aromatic nature of a European pear, it's not surprising that they are the country's most exported pear variety!
Although they are squat in shape (with no discernible neck), these small to medium pears are heavy for their size due to their high water content - deveci pears have been known to reach an astounding 2kg in weight! They have yellowish-green skin that is thin, semi-smooth, and covered with small brown dots, which are indicative of the fruits high sugar content.
Beneath the appealing skin is firm white flesh that emits a glorious floral aroma and is sure to wow your tastebuds: the almost translucent flesh boasts a divinely crisp and crunchy texture and delights eaters with its sublime sweetness and succulence. Indeed, these pears bursting with juice are so well-known for their sugary savour (with almost no acidity) that they've earned the nickname 'honey pear'!
These wonderfully refreshing pears are best enjoyed when simply eaten fresh out of hand as a healthy snack. However, deveci pears are extremely versatile so are perfect for using in any number of recipes! Used fresh, they can combined in fruit salads or made into coleslaw, paired with meats and cheeses on charcuterie boards, blended into smoothies, or pressed into juices. They are commonly cooked too: like other pears, they are delicious when poached and can be simmered with butter and sugar to create sweet caramelized slices. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration!
As well as being divinely delectable, deveci pears are nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are provide a good amount of vitamin C and dietary fibre.

NAME: Pear - fragrant
Description:
Chinese fragrant pears are a must-try for everyone who loves pears!
Fragrant pears have been cultivated in China for over a thousand years, but were only introduced to the wider world in the 2000s. They are a hybrid of two pear varieties - 'Pyrus armeniacifolia', a local Chinese species and the more well-known Asian species 'Pyrus communis'.
At first glance, fragrant pears do not seem significantly different from other pear varieties: they are small in size, round and plump in shape, and have smooth, waxy, and thin skin that is yellow in colour, with brown lenticles and a distinctive red blush.
Yet, as their name indicates, they stand out in aroma. They emit an intense, floral fragrance that fills the room and is sure to wow you! Their flavour is equally as wonderful. Beneath their tender, attractive skin is cream to white-coloured flesh (encasing a few black/brown seeds in the centre) that will delight your tastebuds. Once the fruits are fully ripe, their firm flesh is crisp, succulent, and divinely sweet.
Due to their bite-size stature and wonderfully juicy and crunchy flesh, Chinese fragrant pears have become one of the most favoured pear varieties for eating fresh out of hand. However, they are also ideal for use in a variety of sweet and savoury recipes. For example, you could serve them slightly chilled and pair them with cheese; bake them into tarts and pies, or use them to make revitalizing juice! Additionally, it is popular to poach fragrant pears. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for more recipe inspiration, including caramel pear cookies!
As well as being delectable and versatile, fragrant pears also boast many nutritional benefits. In particular, they are rich in vitamin C and provide a good amount of dietary fibre.

Their flavour is divine, with white flesh that is exquisitely crisp, succulent, and refreshing, and the pears particularly delight the tastebuds with their glorious sweetness (owing to the fact that they have a low acidity in comparison to other pears).
Although best enjoyed simply eaten fresh out of hand, they are also ideal for use in a variety of food and drink creations. Indeed, they work well in any recipe where pears are featured! NAME: Peppers - friggitello
Description:
Add an Italian kick to your dishes with friggitello peppers!
Friggitello peppers are a variety of peppers native to the hot south of Italy. They are small in size and have a smooth, waxy skin that ripens from green to a vibrant red. Underneath the thin skin, the flesh is pale green, encasing a cavity filled with cream-coloured seeds. When picked green, they are subtly sweet with a mild bitterness. When ripened to vibrant red, the friggitello pepper becomes even sweeter with a mild heat to liven up any dish!
Friggitello peppers can be eaten fresh and used in cooking, baking, roasting and sautéing, but in Italy they are best known for frying. This pepper, which is often referred to as the famous frying pepper of Naples can be fried with garlic and light seasonings in olive oil. Traditionally they are served in restaurants with basil, tomatoes and parmesan cheese over crusty bread.
They can also be sliced into salads, grilled, stuffed, and much more! In addition to cooked applications, the peppers can be pickled in white vinegar or dried for extended use.Though friggitello peppers have a complex flavour which is appreciated most when eaten out of hand.
As well as being versatile, our friggitello peppers are also nutritionally valuable. They are an excellent source of vitamins A, B, and C, and also contain essential minerals like potassium, iron and manganese.

Small in size (usually only measuring 2-7cm in length!) and curved or straight in shape, they have shiny, waxy, wrinkled skin that ripens from a deep green to a bright red when fully mature. Beneath this visually appealing skin is crispy, crunchy flesh that envelopes a central hollow space filled with cream-coloured seeds.
Padron peppers have a wonderful fresh aroma and a delicious flavour. They have a vegetal flavour and are ideal for those looking for a way to spice up their diet, wowing your tastebuds with their mild to high level of heat - they range from 500-2,500 SHU on the Scoville scale, with some peppers being significantly spicier than others depending on growing conditions. To enjoy the most complex flavour they can offer, we recommend waiting until they are fully mature, as they will develop a taste that is both sweeter and more intensely spicy!
These peppers can be enjoyed in many different ways: fresh, fried, roasted, grilled, sautéed... the list is endless! Why not follow Spanish tradition by using these bite-sized 'Pimientos de Padron' (as they are known in Spain) in tapas dishes? Simply sear the peppers in a pan with olive oil until the skin blisters, add a sprinkle of salt and a splash of lemon juice, and they are ready to be devoured! They are also the perfect additions to salads, pasta, and soup, and make brilliant pizza toppings. We'd also recommend battering and frying them to make amazing tempura, cooking them into frittatas, and utilising them in rice-based dishes such as paella. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes!
As well as bursting with flavour, padron peppers also boast a range of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are exemplary sources of vitamins C, B6, and K, and contain high levels of dietary fibre, which aids digestion. They also contain potassium and magnesium.

NAME: Persimmon
Description:
Persimmon are an absolute must-try for all exotic fruit lovers!
Stripped of all astringency, Persimmon are small, wonderfully sweet, orange-red fruits originating from Asia, believed to first be cultivated in China in the 7th century (China is still today the largest producer of them!) Cultivation expanded into Japan and Korea, where over 2,000 varieties or cultivars are now listed, they arrived in Europe between the 17th and 19th centuries, and have since become a global phenomenon - did you know that each year around 5 billion kilos of Persimmon are harvested?
We source our Persimmon from Spain and Brazil. Our 'triumph' and 'rojo brillante' varieties are both grown in Spain, with the most important plantations concentrated in the province of Valencia, in the riverside towns on the Xuquer river, particularly Carlet and Alginet. Cultivation of Persimmon in Spain is agriculturally significant, and the rojo brillante persimmon from Ribera del Xúquer has its own D.O.P. (Protected Designation of Origin): farmers in this region have carefully cultivated the fruits using natural techniques since the late 1990s, in order to develop this non-astringent variety.
Popular with growers all over the world, people often at first sight mistake Persimmon for a flat tomato. However, even if in appearance they resemble tomatoes, once you've sampled their juicy flesh you will know you're consuming something totally different! Beneath their glossy, smooth skin is pale orange flesh that ripens from firm and crisp to mouthwateringly succulent and tender, with a complex flavour that delights the tastebuds: within the glorious sweetness are wonderful hints of brown sugar, peach and mango combine to make an amazing taste sensation!
Although best enjoyed simply eaten fresh out of hand, they are very versatile, being suited to a range of culinary applications whether they are firm and dense or have the softness and squishiness of full maturity. We'd especially recommend cooking them into jams and chutneys, adding slices to fruit salads, chopping them into salsas, and incorporating them into sweet baked goods such as tarts and pies! You can even dry them to turn them into a chewy snack! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipes, including Persimmon chiffon pie!
As well as being delicious, Persimmon boast a range of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre, vitamin C, and magnesium, and are rich in many nutrients, including copper, iron, calcium, and phosphorus.

Love pineapples? Our two varieties of baby pineapples - phulae pineapples (also known as 'Phu Lae') from the Nang Lae district of Thailand and Queen Victoria pineapples from Bangladesh and Mauritius - are just the thing for you!
In appearance, baby pineapples are almost identical to regular pineapples, varying only in their slightly more rounded shape and miniature size. Called 'baby' pineapples, it's no surprise that they are much smaller than pineapples you can find in supermarkets - they typically measure approximately 5 inches long and 3 inches wide.
Like their larger sister fruits, they have an intense fragrance that fills the room, with many regarding them as more aromatic than regular pineapples. Beneath their eye-catching, golden outer casing is yellow flesh which delights the tastebuds with its sugar-sweet taste, containing little to no acidity. As well as being favoured for their succulence and sweetness, baby pineapples are also loved by exotic fruit fans due to the fact that they have a much softer core than regular pineapples - unlike supermarket-bought pineapples, you can easily eat the core, and do not need to discard it! Our phulae pineapples are especially juicy and sweet, and are accordingly one of the most popular pineapples in Thailand, which is impressive considering the country cultivates at least 27 different varieties of the fruit! Indeed, phulae pineapples are a rare and expensive delicacy in their native Thailand, where they are sold at 10 times the price of other pineapples due to their superior flavour!
The best way to enjoy this wonderful fruit is to simply devour the flesh. For instance, on the streets of Southeast Asian countries, pieces of baby pineapple are sold as refreshing snacks to provide much-needed coolness and hydration in the scorching summer months. However, there are innumerable culinary applications for baby pineapple, with these versatile fruits suiting both sweet and savoury recipes! They are perfect for adding some tropical flavour to fruit salads and creating stunning smoothies, and taste divine when served grilled with chicken. These divinely delectable fruits are best enjoyed when simply eaten fresh out of hand, particularly because they are less acidic and less fibrous than other varieties. NAME: Pineapple - Pina MD2
Description:
Pineapple MD2, which was first commercially grown in the 1980s, was developed to satisfy demand for fresh pineapples with exceptional sweetness as well as uniformity and consistency in size and ripeness.
Compared to other pineapple cultivars, MD2 is considered superior because the uniform bright gold colour, sweeter taste, four-times Vitamin C content, lower fibre, lower acidity and smaller fruits on average at about 2-2.5kg each.
Due to its superior eating qualities, MD2 commands around three times the price of other more commonly found pineapple varieties.
The journey of this variety from idea to development can be traced back to 1961 when the Pineapple Research Institute (PRI) in Hawaii was funded by a consortium of companies formed by Dole, Del Monte and Maui Pineapple Company to select and breed a new superior pineapple.
In 1975, Maui Pineapple Company took responsibility for the hybrids developed at the PRI. MD2 was originally known as 73- 114 but later renamed MD2, in honour of Millie Dillard, the wife of the then General Manager of the pineapple company.

Description:
Love plums and mangoes? Our plum mangoes are just the things for you!
Plum mangoes, also known as 'Maprong mangoes' and 'Marian plums', are closely related to the mango.
They are small fruits and have a size and shape roughly comparable to an egg. They have thin, smooth skin that ripens from green to a dazzlingly bright orange-yellow hue.
Although in appearance plum mangoes do not resemble their namesakes, once you cut into the flesh you will realise how they gained their title. The first hint is given by their aroma: the fruits emit a divine mango-like fragrance that wows your senses.
It is the flesh's flavour and texture though that really give plum mangoes their name. In texture, the fruits are often said to be comparable to plums: the orange flesh (encasing a bitter but edible central seed) offers an initial crispy bite, but then reveals its soft, jelly-like (and slightly fibrous) texture. In flavour, however, the fruits are regularly likened to mangoes, as they delight the tastebuds with a sweet taste and subtle notes of tartness.
Whilst plum mangoes are most commonly eaten fresh out of hand, they are ideal for a number of culinary uses. We'd recommend adding them to fruit salads and using them to make mouthwatering pickles, chutneys, and compotes. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for more recipe inspiration.
As well as being delicious, plum mangoes boast a number of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre and vitamin C.

Description:
Love apricots and plums? Then we have just the thing for you!
Pluots, also known as 'apriums', are the delicious result of an experimental hybridisation of plums and apricots undertaken in the 1980s.
If you look at their genetic composition, you will see that they are technically more plum than apricot: there are many varieties of pluot but they are usually approximately 70-75% plum and 25-30% apricot. In appearance too pluots have more than a passing resemblance to plums, owing to their round shape and smooth, crunchy skin - pluots' skin ranges from pinkish-red and dark purple to bright green, depending on which variety of plum they derive from - and their delightfully fragrant aroma is reminiscent of both fruits.
Yet, the texture of pluots' flesh is more closely aligned to that of apricots, and in taste too apricot shines through. Rather than the bitterness that can sometimes be found in plums, pluots' extremely juicy, yellow to crimson flesh boasts a unique, intense flavour and a sweetness that is utterly mouthwatering,
Delectable when eaten fresh out of hand, pluots are also ideal for making chutneys, jams, and sweet, healthy smoothies, for adding some flavour to your morning granola or porridge, and especially suit baking: we recommend using them to bake delectable pies, tarts, cobblers, and cakes! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some enticing recipes!
On top of their appetizing flavour, pluots are additionally nutritionally valuable: they are a good source of fibre, potassium, and vitamin C.

NAME: Pomegranate
Description:
Pomegranates are a must-try for all fruit lovers!
Round in shape and medium in size, our pomegranates from Peru somewhat resemble apples in appearance. However, what's underneath the surface makes pomegranates stand out from the crowd. Beneath their smooth, glossy red skin is an abundance of white seeds encased in ruby-red sacs! These sacs, known as arils, are not only completely eye-catching - they almost look like jewels! - but the flesh contained in them is also supremely delicious. The skin and pith should not be eaten.
Once you've removed the sacs from the pith, the succulent flesh can be eaten raw - the arils have a taste similar to cranberries, with a sharpness complemented by delicate notes of sweetness. The arils are also commonly juiced to make a refreshing beverage. Although these are the two most typical uses, pomegranates can be used in any number of recipes. We'd particularly recommend scattering the sacs over cereals and oatmeal, incorporating them in salads, and using them to decorate meat and fish dishes. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipes, including an orange and pomegranate cheesecake!
As well as being delectable and versatile, pomegranates have in recent years become renowned for their nutritional benefits. Commonly regarded as a super food, they are packed with antioxidants and are an excellent source of dietary fibre.

Consumed in a similar way to other potato varieties, Jersey Royal potatoes are especially well suited to roasting, boiling, and baking. Why not follow local Jersey tradition and boil them in salt water before serving them with fresh mint and butter? They are also ideal for adding some subtle sweetness to salads, curries, and soups, and we'd recommend using them to make hearty shepherd pies and incorporating slices into gratins and casseroles. Not only are sweet potatoes one of the oldest-cultivated foods in the world - remnants of sweet potatoes have been found that date back over 8000 years! - but they are also one of the healthiest, with purple sweet potatoes in particular being hailed as a 'superfood' due to their supposed ability to extend life expectancy!
In shape, purple sweet potatoes resemble other sweet potato varieties. However, they excel in flavour. Although their deep purple flesh is denser and drier than most sweet potato varieties, it wows the tastebuds with its intensely rich flavour that combines both sweet and savoury notes and boasts an almost wine-like savour! Once boiled and coated with a tad of melted butter, these potatoes gain a delightfully creamy texture, making them simply divine!
Purple sweet potatoes' starchy texture means they are best suited to cooked applications such as boiling, mashing, frying, or baking, although please note that their crumbly flesh takes longer to cook than that of regular potatoes. They are also ideal for adding some subtle sweetness to salads, curries, and soups, and are perfect for bringing eye-catching colour to your mealtimes, such as dazzling purple jacket potatoes and chips! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including a scrumptious purple sweet potato pie!
As well as being supremely delectable, purple sweet potatoes are renowned for being far more nutritious than supermarket-bought potatoes, boasting a higher content of dietary fibre and being lower in both carbohydrates and calories! Purple sweet potatoes also contain anthocyanin (the natural compound that gives the potatoes their striking purple hue!), a powerful antioxidant linked to numerous health benefits, and they are additionally rich in potassium, iron, folate, and vitamins A and C.

NAME: Potato - purple, 'violetta', 'valfi' & 'vitelotte'
Description:
Vitelotte, violetta, and valfi potatoes are some of the most visually appealing and nutritionally valuable potato varieties that we sell!
These purple potatoes, which owe their name to their dazzling deep purple/dark blue skin and flesh, are regarded by many as gourmet delicacies - indeed, vitelotte potatoes are so rare and highly prized that they have gained the nickname 'truffle potatoes'!
They all are generally medium in size (although vitelotte can sometimes be smaller) and they all have flesh that, concealed beneath smooth (violetta) or bumpy (valfi and vitelotte) skin, has a denser texture and a slightly nuttier, earthier flavour than a white potato. Once cooked, the flesh of all three varieties is floury yet smooth (violettas have the fluffiest texture of the three), and has a delicious flavour somewhat reminiscent of chestnuts. If you are looking for a sweeter potato, we would recommend the violetta, as these have subtle undertones of sweetness, whereas if you are looking for a potato with a more distinctive, spicier flavour we would suggest choosing valfi potatoes.
Consumed in a similar way to other potato varieties, purple potatoes are very versatile and will suit all of your culinary needs. However, they are arguably most well-suited for boiling, mashing, baking, and frying; we would recommend keeping the skins on during cooking so you can retain the eye-catching colour! As the flesh retains much of its vibrant purple hue even once cooked, purple potatoes are perfect for adding some colour to your mealtimes - we would suggest making spectacular purple roast and mashed potatoes; adding purple potato to your salads to boost their healthiness; making use of their drier texture to make potato pancakes and gnocchi, and boiling and pureeing them to make purple soup. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipes - we would especially suggest the violetta gratin and smashed vitelotte potatoes recipes!
Vitelotte, violetta, and valfi potatoes stand out in terms of their health benefits. As well as being, like other potatoes, an excellent source of fibre and potassium, and a good provider of iron, folate, and vitamins C and B6, these potatoes are also uniquely rich in anti-oxidants - valfi potatoes contain around 30% more anti-oxidants than white potatoes! - such as anthocyanin, which is believed to boost the immune system.

NAME: Potato - Red Duke of York
Description:
Red Duke of York potatoes are one of the fluffiest potato varieties you can buy!
First cultivated in the UK in 1942, these potatoes were a favourite among home gardeners during World War Two and have been popular ever since.

Indeed, their flesh has such a high content of dry matter that they are regarded by many chefs as the fluffiest potatoes! This delicious flesh has a fresh, earthy flavour.
Consumed in a similar way to other potato varieties, Red Duke of York potatoes are perfect for roasting - make sure to keep the skins on during cooking so you can retain the eye-catching colour and wow your family and friends with red-skinned roast potatoes! They are also ideal for mashing and making heavenly fluffy gnocchi. Indeed, they are a great all-rounder - there are so many ways you can use them to add some colour and sweetness to your mealtimes, from boiling to wedging to using them as salad potatoes. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes!
Red Duke of York potatoes boast a number of health benefits. Like other potatoes, they are an excellent source of fibre and potassium, and a good provider of iron, folate, and vitamins C and B6.

The firm flesh has, once cooked, a delightfully tender, fluffy texture and a delectably sweet, buttery flavour with fresh, earthy undertones.
Consumed in a similar way to other potato varieties, Shetland black potatoes are particularly well-suited to sautéing, boiling, and roasting - they make especially scrumptious crisps and chips! They are also excellent at absorbing flavours from sauces and gravies and are ideal accompaniments to meats such as cider pork chops. Like other potatoes, Shetland black potatoes are an excellent source of fibre and potassium, and also provide good amounts of iron, folate, and vitamins C and B6.

NAME: Potato - yukon gold
Description:
Although first developed in Canada and named after the country's Yukon River, Yukon Gold potatoes are today one of the most popular potato varieties in the world - they were even the preferred potato of The Obamas when they were in the White House!
Yukon Gold potatoes are medium to large in size and have a slightly flatter shape than other varieties. Beneath their delicate, speckled, golden skin is golden-yellow flesh that is firm and moist. When cooked, Yukon Gold potatoes take on a creamy and tender consistency that delights the tastebuds: their melt-in-the-mouth flesh astounds with its buttery, earthy flavour, especially because they boast distinctive notes of sweetness.
These potatoes can be consumed in any way you'd eat other potato varieties, from roasting and baking to mashing and boiling. Did you know that they were the potato of choice for the dauphinoise at the state dinner, and that 600 kilograms of Yukon Gold potatoes were also used at the Oscars award show in 2016 where Wolfgang Puck served the tubers with crème Fraiche and Caspian caviar? They are particularly favoured by chefs because they retain their eye-catching golden hue even when cooked! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for a recipe for divine garlic mashed potatoes!
As well as being delicious and versatile, Yukon Gold potatoes are an excellent source of vitamin C - they contain nearly twice as much vitamin C as a regular baking potato! - are rich in dietary fibre and potassium, and provide a good amount of calcium.

Ingredients- 900g yukon gold potatoes, washed and quartered- 4 cloves garlic- salt- 350ml double cream, warm- 110g butter, cold
MethodPlace the potatoes and garlic in a large saucepan. Cover with 1 to 2 inches of cold water and season generously with salt. The water should taste like the sea. Taste it! If the water is under-seasoned at this point, it will be hard to have a well seasoned end product. Bring the pot of water to a boil and cook until the potatoes are fork-tender, about 20 to 25 minutes. Drain the potatoes and garlic well. Bring the heavy cream to a boil in a small saucepan. Once the cream has come to a boil remove from the heat. While the potatoes are still hot, add a third of the cream and butter then stir vigorously into the potatoes. Repeat this process two more times until all the cream and butter has incorporated. Taste the potatoes for seasoning and add salt, if needed. Serve immediately or cover with foil and keep warm in the oven on a low heat.

NAME: Prekese

One of its most common uses is to spice Banga soup which is a type of palm fruit soup. It's also used in pepper soup and in Ghana, soft drinks have been flavoured with this versatile fruit.
The fruit is regularly used as a dietary supplement rich in vitamins. The therapeutic properties of the plant have been documented since 1948 and authenticated in laboratory and field experiments.
Prekese is rich in protein, lipids, potassium, iron, magnesium, phosphorous, and vitamin C.

NAME: Quince
Description:
Quinces are a must-try for all exotic fruit lovers!
Originating from Turkestan and Persia, quinces are now grown all over Europe.
Although raw quinces are inedible, they are nevertheless renowned - they are highly regarded for their aroma, upheld as superb natural air fresheners. Try leaving a quince in the glove box of your car and benefit from the wonderful fragrance for many months!
However, they offer more than an intense aroma! Known as 'apple' or 'pear' quinces depending upon their shape, the skin of these medium to large-sized fruits ripens to an eye-catching golden yellow. Beneath their appealing skin is dense cream to yellow coloured flesh that is astringent and sour but, once cooked, gains a delicious floral flavour with notes of honey! Indeed, quince is a highly prized fruit in Spain due to the popularity of 'membrillo', the delectable quince paste that results from boiling the fruits with sugar! After boiling, it is cooled, cut into squares and served with soft cheeses or as a candy.
Despite being best suited for making jams, preserves, pastes, and jellies, which pair wonderfully with poultry, beef and game, quinces are also perfect ingredients when making baked goods such as cakes and are also often infused with spirits including vodka and grappa! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including a scrumptious quince crumble tart!
As well as being versatile, quinces are nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre and provide a good amount of vitamin C and potassium.

NAME: Rambutan
Description:
A popular fruit from Southeast Asia, rambutan is a must-try for any exotic fruit lover!
Rambutan fruits are small in size - they usually measure only 3-5cm in diameter - and round to oval in shape. They get their name from the Malay word 'Rambut', which means 'hair': one look at these unique fruits and you will understand why! Their firm, leathery, reddish-pink skin is covered in soft spikes known as 'pinterns' which give them a wild, 'hairy' appearance. Indeed, in Vietnamese, rambutan is known as 'chôm chôm', which translates to 'messy hair'!
Beneath the dazzling exterior of these wonderfully aromatic fruits is tender, pinkish-white flesh that will delight your tastebuds with its brilliant flavour. The flesh is chewy and supremely succulent and boasts a sweet, fruity savour with notes of strawberries and grapes and is complemented by subtly acidic undertones. We would describe the flavour as a delightful mix of lychee and pineapple!
Although rambutans are best enjoyed when eaten fresh out of hand (simply discard the skin and central seed), they can also be utilised in a range of sweet and savoury food and drink recipes! The flesh is perfect for combining in fruit salads, topping ice cream and sorbets, imparting some sweetness to curries and soups, and simmering into jams! They are also ideal for creating bright, floral cocktails and mocktails! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including a healthy rambutan smoothie!
As well as being divinely delectable and versatile, rambutans are nutritionally valuable too. In particular, they are good sources of vitamin C and copper.

Description:
Ramontchi is highly nutritious and the fruit, leaves and bark have many uses in traditonal medicine. Ramonthi grow on a flowering plant native to much of Africa and tropical and temperate parts of Asia. Its seeds are heavily distributed by birds resulting in a very wide distribution of the species. Therer are usually 3 to 10 small seeds per fruit. The pulp is yellow to orange and sweet when fully ripe but with an acidic tang if eaten before maturity. Prior to eating, fruits are massaged to soften the flesh, then consumed whole or by squeezing the flesh out.

Rose apples are a refreshing fruit from South Asia with a delicate flavour and crisp texture.
An aesthetically appealing fruit, rose apples have a distinctively elongated, bell-like shape and their skin boasts a glossy shine. The smooth, delicate skin has a wax like texture, which is the reason why the fruit is often referred to as 'wax apple'.
Beneath their attractive exterior is white or pink flesh which is fragrant, crisp, and extremely juicy. In fact, rose apples are one of the most succulent fruits we've ever tried: they consist of over 90% water, so it's not surprising that these 'water apples' are considered ideal for quenching thirst! The usually seedless flesh is subtly sweet, offering hints of watermelon and apple flavour.
Whilst immature green rose apples are perfect for making delicious pickles and chutneys and combining into salads, the riper red-skinned fruits are usually eaten fresh out of hand (especially because you don't need to peel them!)

NAME: Safou
Description:
Want to try a fruit that has a taste comparable to a unique combination of green olive and avocado? Then you need to try safou!
These nutritious fruits native to West and Central Africa are typically small to medium in size and elongated in shape. They immediately catch the eye with their attractive, glossy, purple to bluish/black skin.
Beneath their smooth skin is soft flesh which varies in colour, ranging from green and brownish/cream to shades of pink. As well as wowing with its tender texture and citrus-like fragrance, the flesh astounds with its versatility: when eaten fresh, it has a wonderfully acidic flavour, whereas when it's roasted or quickly boiled in salted water, the pulp separates from the skin and long, brown, central seed and takes on a more gentle tangy, nutty flavour and an amazingly buttery texture. With the nickname 'butterfruit', it's not surprising that the flesh is velvety smooth!
Due to the mellower flavour and melt-in-the-mouth texture, safou is traditionally eaten cooked. It is typically eaten as a snack between meals, however in Nigeria, cooked safou pulp is combined with starchy foods like maize to make a hearty main course! Once the seed has been removed, you can stuff the fruit with cooked meats, spices, and vegetables for a real taste sensation, or why not try pureeing the pulp into a dip to serve with crisps and chips? Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including delectable roast tomatoes with safou!
Like its namesake butter, safou is high in fats and very calorie-dense. However, safou boasts nutritional benefits too: it has a high content of amino acids, the chemical building blocks of proteins, and is rich in potassium, calcium, and magnesium.

NAME: Santol 'wild mangosteen'
Description:
If you love mangosteens then you need to try santol, the 'wild mangosteen' native to Cambodia, Laos, and Malaya!
Santols are small, round to oval-shaped fruits with golden yellow peel that is fuzzy and leathery, comparable to the skin of a peach. When you look beneath their wrinkled skin, you will understand why santol is also known as the 'cotton fruit' - they have wonderfully fluffy white flesh that is soft, spongy, and juicy. As with mangosteens, the flesh of santols never entirely separates from the internal, inedible seeds that it surrounds. Sucking the flesh provides an astounding sweet-sour flavour that delights the tastebuds, with their milky, creamy, sweetish juice being offset by tart, floral, and citrus notes! The ratio of sweet to sour varies depending upon the variety: the sweetest santol fruit has a sugary savour, with undertones of apple and peach, whilst a sour santol provides a distinctive umami flavour.
Although best enjoyed when simply eaten fresh out of hand, santols are also well-suited to a range of culinary applications. For instance, their flesh can be used to make spectacular jams, jellies, and chutneys, can be blended into smoothies, and is often candied! Santols' rind is also sometimes dried and then ground into a powder and some people pickle it for use as a souring agent. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite santol recipes!
As well as being supremely delectable, santols also provide many nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre and iron, and are rich in calcium and vitamin C.

NAME: Sapodilla 'caramel'
Description:
The caramel sapodilla is a superior variety from Vietnam which are around 3 to 4 times larger than the sapodilla we sell that come from Thailand and India. The texture of the Vietnamese sapodilla is perfectly smooth, one of the softest and smoothest fruits you will ever try.
The flavour is divine, reminiscent of caramel and brown sugar and the reason we put the caramel sapodilla in our list of top 10 fruits! Simply wait to ripen then eat out of hand or mix in a blender with almond milk and cinammon for the ultimate smoothie.
Sapodilla was imported to Vietnam a long time ago. In the last 20 years, sapodilla has been widely planted in the north, where it grew for the first time in Xuan Dinh, Tu Liem district, Hanoi.
Sapodilla fruit is shaped like an egg and weighs from 10 to 200 grams. Its peel is brown with tiny cracks near the stalk. The pulp, which is brown and yellow, is very juicy and smells very sweet. When it is not ripe, it is not edible because it contains a lot of sticky resin.
There are two popular species of sapodilla grown in Vietnam: orange pulp and white-yellow pulp sapodilla. The orange pulp sapodilla is planted in the north on the highlands. The pulp of the white-yellow sapodilla is light yellow or yellow and the peel is green or yellow. The peel is thin; the pulp is soft and has taste of peach, banana, and apple.
Sapodilla flower consecutively bloom in bunches so that it has fruits to offer throughout the year.

Also known as 'green caviar' due to their caviar-like appearance, sea grapes are actually a type of seaweed. Don't let that put you off though! Both are sure to wow your tastebuds though! Sea grapes are usually eaten raw once they've been soaked in and rinsed with water - follow the instructions on the packet (also listed in the preparation and usage sections below) to make sure you prepare and use them correctly.
After preparation, they are perfect for incorporating into a variety of dishes, from salads to sushi, rice, and noodles! They pair particularly well with wasabi and sesame sauces. However you use them, they will definitely bring freshness and a notable textural contrast to your meals!
As well as this, they are rich in fibre and contain an array of other healthful nutrients and minerals too, including calcium, iron, and magnesium.

Description:
Sea Moss is a species of red algae which grows abundantly along the rocky parts of the Atlantic coast of Europe and North America.
Our sea moss is from the Caribbean islands and sold in 100g packets (unprocessed) and 50g packets (natural debris removed, cleaned and separated into small pieces). You'll notice that the price for the 50g packets is almost the same as the 100g packets as it's particularly time-consuming to clean and sort the sea moss once it's been removed from the ocean.
It's an industrial source of carrageenan, which is the main reason for cultivation however due to a high nutrient density, it's also grown and dried then exported around the world to be used as a healthy supplement to a balanced diet.
Culinary uses of sea moss vary across the world. In Ireland and parts of Scotland, it's boiled in milk and strained, before sugar and other flavourings such as vanilla, cinnamon, brandy, or whiskey are added. The end product is a kind of jelly similar to pannacotta.
Similarly, in Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago, it's boiled with cinnamon and milk to make a thick drink called Irish moss that is believed to be an aphrodisiac.
In Venezuela it has been used for generations as a home remedy for sore throat and chest congestion, boiled in milk and served with honey before bed.

NAME: Snake fruit - salacca, Thailand
Description:
Salak is a species of palm tree native to Java and Sumatra in Indonesia.
The taste is usually sweet and acidic at the same time, but its apple-like texture can vary from very dry and crumbly (salak pondoh from Yogyakarta) to moist and crunchy (salak Bali). The taste is often compared to a rich pineapple flavour with a hint of fizziness.
The fruits grow in clusters at the base of the palm, and are also known as snake fruit due to the reddish-brown scaly skin.
They are about the size and shape of a ripe fig, with a distinct tip. The pulp is edible. The fruit can be peeled by pinching the tip, which should cause the skin to slough off so it can be pulled away.
The fruit inside consists of two or three lobes with the two larger ones, or even all three, containing a large inedible seed. The lobes resemble, and have the consistency of, large peeled garlic cloves.
As well as being delicious, salacca boasts numerous health benefits. In particular, it is extremely rich in iron, providing 30% of your daily required amount, and provides a good amount of vitamin C.

NAME: Snake fruit - salak pondoh, Indonesia
Description:
Salak is the fruit of a species of palm tree, native to Java and Sumatra in Indonesia. Snake fruit, as it's also called, thanks to its brown scaly skin, has a good keep quality. Peeling the thin skin will reveal 3 lobes, cream to yellow in colour containing 2 or 3 inedibe seeds. They are about the size and shape of a mature fig. The taste can be compared to that of an apple and pineapple.
The texture varies between cultivars, salak pondoh having a crisp and crunchy feel in the mouth.
Salak pondoh is grown in abundance in the Yogyakarta province on the island of Java, Indonesia. It's popularity in Indonesia, compared to other cultivars, is mainly due to the intensity of its aroma the well balanced sweet flavour and low cost.
There are three commonly found cultivars of salak which are pondoh, bali and gula pasir. Typically, pondoh are the largest in size.

Combined, these three jewels of the Caribbean come together to make a splendid tropical drink! Simply brew one of the conveniently-packed teabags in a cup of boiling water for 1-2 minutes, and then your tea will be ready!
As well as being packed with flavour, this tea boasts many nutritional benefits. It's 100% natural, containing no additives, preservatives, or flavourings, and will add 0 calories and 0g of sugar to your diet!

NAME: Star apple - fresh and frozen
Description:
Star apples are a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
Star apples are small to medium in size - they usually measure about 5-10cm in diameter - and perfectly round in shape. They have delicate, glossy skin that ripens to either a vibrant green or a dazzling purple hue.
Beneath their smooth, attractive skin is a thin layer of rind: the rind is dark purple in purple star apples, whereas in green star apples it is white. Whilst the rind of purple star apples is typically much thicker, please note that in both varieties the rind contains a sticky latex that is inedible.
At the core of these aromatic fruits is tender, white or purple pulp that wows with its radiating star pattern (hence the nickname 'star apple'!) The soft pulp excites the tastebuds too with its delicious flavour: once you've discarded the inedible seeds, you can enjoy the sweet, juicy jelly-like flesh and be delighted by its combination of notes of lychee, persimmons, and rambutans! For those with a sweet tooth, we'd particularly recommend the purple star apples, as these are usually packed with more sweetness, however some fruit fans prefer green star apples due to their thinner skin and slightly greater density of pulp.
Star apples are best enjoyed when simply eaten fresh out of hand, especially because this is the optimal way to savour the fruits' sweet milky juice! Yet they are also perfect for use in any number of sweet and savoury recipes. They are particularly ideal for combining in fruit salads, incorporating into ceviche, blending into smoothies, and making sorbet! They are also well-suited for baking, making a wonderful pastry filling, and can even be used to flavour teas and cocktails! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including the famous Jamaican fruit salad known as 'matrimony' that combines condensed milk and flavourful tart fruits including grapefruits, star apples, and oranges!
As well as being supremely delectable, star apples boast many nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and calcium and provide a good amount of phosphorous.

NAME: Starfruit
Description:
Starfruit (also known as 'carambola') is a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
As you have probably guessed, these fruits are best known for their distinctive appearance. These medium-sized, waxy-skinned fruits have 5 ridged edges, so when they are sliced crossways, the slices are shaped like stars (hence their name)!
However, it is not only their eye-catching appearance that delights the senses - starfruit's flavour is similarly spectacular!
When they are picked before they've reached full maturity, starfruits are firm and green with a crisp, citrus-like flavour. At this stage, they primarily impart sour notes, so they are ideal for salads and stir-fries. Yet, if left to ripen fully, starfruits turn a dazzling bright yellow in colour and they soften significantly. Once completely mature, starfruits are succulent and crisp, and boast a divine sweet-tart savour, with delectable notes of grape and plum!
Ripe starfruits are best enjoyed when simply eaten fresh out of hand, especially because the entire fruit is edible, including the small, brown seeds! Slices are also popularly combined in fruit salads. The fruits are also perfect for juicing - indeed, in Brazil, starfruit juice is renowned as an excellent thirst quencher! Starfruit juice is also an excellent addition to cocktails and slices of starfruit make brilliant cocktail garnishes! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including a scrumptious starfruit bruschetta!
Furthermore, starfruits are nutritionally beneficial. In particular, they are extremely rich in vitamin C - one starfruit provides half your daily required vitamin C content! - provide great amounts of vitamin K, and are a good source of dietary fibre.

NAME: Stinking toe
Description:
The fruit of the West Indian locust tree may just win the award for the most unappealing nickname given to a fruit! It's nickname, 'stinking toe' is not without reason however, the pods are toe-shaped and some say the flesh inside stinks like feet. Much like the notorious durian fruit though, the smell of stinking toe is regarded as 'love it or hate it' so just as many people are fond of it as dislike it. Fortunately, the outer shell of the stinking toe is very hard, keeping the majority of the odour at bay until it's cracked with a strong knife or hammer.
Stinking toe matures during the rainy seasons and is then harvested during summer months. The presence of an unusual odour is actually a sign of ripeness.
The dry powdery cream coloured pulp, which resembles flour or icing sugar, has a sweet taste - some people say it tastes like dried milk. The miniature soluble fibers dissolve easily in water or milk, which it naturally thickens.
Whilst it can be enjoyed raw, it's often used in baking, blending, or cooking.
In Jamaica, where the fruit grows wild, locals blend the pulp with water, sugar, and spices to make a refreshing beverage.
In Brazil, where the fruit is known as jatobá, bakers use the dried powder of the pulp to make a biscuit-like pastry known as a broinha.
Stinking toe is considered one of the richest natural foods in the plant kingdom because of its high concentration of starches and proteins. Throughout Central and South America, the fruit is prized for its purported medicinal benefits. Its rumored to be everything from an aphrodisiac to a remedy for diarrhea.
The seeds are dispersed with the help of the agouti, a tropical rodent with teeth strong enough to break open the pods. They often carry the fruits to other areas and bury them for later. Forgotten fruits germinate and grow into new trees. It's thanks to the agouti, that stinking toe is now found throughout much of the Caribbean, Central America, and South America.

NAME: Stone apple (bael)
Description:
Bael is an amazing fruit that has long been used in South Asian cuisine!
Round to oval in shape and small to medium in size, the bael fruit, also known as bilva, has a thick, hard, grey, green or yellow shell which takes some effort to crack. Indeed, the outer shell is so tough that the fruit has gained the nickname 'stone apple'!
However, the delicious flesh underneath is well worth the effort! Tamarinds are bean-like pods with a light to dark brown exterior shell. Beneath their hard, smooth, outer casing is soft flesh that surrounds shiny black seeds - as the fruits mature, the flesh dehydrates and takes the form of a paste.
It is at this stage of advanced maturity that the flesh acquires the best flavour: the fully ripened flesh mellows in sourness and instead becomes sweeter, wowing the tastebuds with its wonderful mixture of notes of dates and raisins. Some people even compare their flavour to that of Coca-Cola!
The small size and sweet flavour of tamarinds means they are perfect for snacking. However, they are more commonly used in recipes - indeed, they are a staple ingredient in Thai cuisine! The pasty flesh is perfect for complementing the spicy notes of curries and is used in Pad Thai, one of Thailand's most famous dishes! Sweet tamarinds are ideal for making drinks too: simply soak the flesh in a small amount of warm water for 10 minutes and then remove the seeds and fibre. After that, blend the flesh with cold water and sugar until smooth and then strain! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including a scrumptious beef stew in tamarind sauce!
As well as being delicious, sweet tamarinds boast numerous nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin B and are rich in calcium.

It takes the name velvet tamarind because of the smooth, soft velvet-like exterior.
The small, thin pods are easily cracked to reveal a dry, powdery flesh which surrounds a small, shiny central seed.
The flesh is delicious and enjoyable to eat. Its flavour is like candy and has some resemblance to the more commonly found sweet tamarind (known as 'tamarindus indica').
The seeds and pod are not eaten.
Our velvet tamarind from Sri Lanka tends to be smaller than our other varieties. They have a thin layer of flesh that boasts a sweet-sour flavour, with the tangy notes usually dominating. If you're looking for sweeter fruits, we'd recommend our velvet tamarind from Nigeria.

NAME: Turmeric
Description:
Looking for a way to add a kick of spice to your mealtimes? Our fresh turmeric is just the thing for you!
Fresh turmeric is elongated and slender in shape, somewhat resembling a long finger, and has brownish-orange skin that is thin, rough, and marked with wrinkles and knobs. Beneath this textured skin is eye-catching bright orange flesh that will wow your tastebuds with its delicious flavour: it has distinctive warming properties and wonderful peppery notes, with strong undertones of carrot and ginger. Did you know it is one of the ingredients that constitutes curry powder?
Although most often boiled and dried to create turmeric powder, fresh turmeric can also be fried and pickled, and is perfect for adding gentle freshness to curries. Its colour alone is enough to make turmeric a superior culinary ingredient - it is sure to brighten up any dish! Indeed, it is also known as 'Indian saffron' because it is often used in Indian cuisine as a substitute for saffron in bringing some visual vibrancy. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including an extremely healthy tropical turmeric smoothie!
As well as being versatile and delectable, turmeric also boasts many nutritional benefits. In particular, its primary active ingredient, curcumin, has powerful anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties that have made the spice popular in Chinese and Ayurvedic medicines for centuries.
We also have organic and fair trade turmeric from small-scale farmers deep in Peru.

NAME: Wampee fruit
Description:
We doubt even our most knowledgeable exotic fruit connoisseurs have heard of the little-known wampee fruit!
Wampee fruits are the very small fruits of the wampee tree, an evergreen tree found most commonly in Southeast Asia. The fruits are oval in shape and have smooth, thin, golden-yellow skin. They are very similar in appearance to lychee, but are actually part of the citrus family!
Beneath this eye-catching skin is delicate and supremely succulent white flesh that has an enticing floral aroma and a divine sweetness that is complemented by pleasant sour notes. Within the flesh, there are several medium-sized seeds, which are typically discarded. The skin can be eaten though, and we'd recommend doing so, because otherwise you'll miss its spicy flavour!
Wampee are best enjoyed when simply eaten fresh out of hand. However, they are also well-suited to a number of culinary applications. When the skins are kept on, the fruits have a unique umami flavour that makes them ideal for sweet and savoury dishes. We'd particularly recommend cooking them with meat-based dishes and using them to make thirst-quenching drinks - look in the 'Further information' tab below for a recipe for a wampee fruit martini!

NAME: Wood apple (kodbel)
Description:
A fruit that is considered so sacred in India that it is offered to the god Ganesh, wood apples are a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
Wood apples are small to medium in size and round (often perfectly spherical) in shape. From the exterior they somewhat resemble small coconuts: they have an extremely hard, rough brown shell that needs to be hit firmly with the back of a cleaver to be cracked.
Beneath this tough shell is a surprising interior! The brown flesh inside showcases an array of textures due to its combination of seeds and long, stringy fibres - we'd describe the texture as creamy, moist, and slightly crunchy and grainy. The flavour is unique too, with the moist, sticky, and fibrous pulp combining sweet and savoury notes and musky undertones. We'd liken the savour to an unusual mix of tamarind, raisins, and cheese! Everything inside the shell is edible, however the fibres and seeds are discarded by some.
With a fragrance comparable to raisins and blue cheese and an unmatched flavour profile, it's safe to say that eating the flesh simply fresh out of hand is a real experience! However, for the best enjoyment of these wonderful fruits, we'd recommend using them to make delectable juices and chutneys, as is common in their native Sri Lanka and India - check out the 'Further information' tab below for a recipe for an amazing wood apple chutney! In Sri Lanka, wood apple flesh is popularly mixed with coconut milk and palm sugar to create a sweet, slightly acidic beverage that is an ideal thirst-quencher in hot weather. Indeed, they make spectacular fruity milkshakes and smoothies!
As well as being versatile, wood apples have long been a staple of Ayurvedic medicine, and they are still today consumed for their nutritional benefits. In particular, they are rich in dietary fibre and vitamin C and provide good amounts of calcium and iron.

Description:
Chinese yams are delicious vegetables that are full of healthful nutrients and vitamins!
Despite their name, we source these yams from France - yams have been grown on the banks of the River Loire for over 100 years! Beneath this thick, cylindrical vegetable's tough, brown skin is delectable, starchy white/cream-coloured flesh, that has an earthy, largely neutral, flavour - Chinese yams have slightly softer flesh than other yams, and are fresher rather than sweet in taste. When cooked, the earthy flavour is mellowed, and the taste becomes comparable to that of potatoes, with notes of chestnut.
Yams are staples of millions of people's cuisine, typically consumed in a similar fashion to how we consume potatoes in the UK. We too would recommend using them as you would usually use potatoes: you could make a gratin, with bechamel sauce and grated cheese; superb French fries, and mash or roast them. There are so many ways to use these versatile vegetables! They are a perfect way of adding texture to soups, stews, and casseroles, and their mild taste means they are also excellent at soaking up the flavour of spices. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including wonderful Cantonese pork soup with yam and carrots!
Additionally, Chinese yams boast a range of nutritional benefits. Used for centuries in traditional medicine, they are still today vaunted as excellent sources of dietary fibre, and are also highly regarded for their richness in iron, calcium, potassium, and vitamin B1.

NAME: Yam - white
Description:
White yams are delicious vegetables that are cultivated in many parts of the world, primarily in countries in Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean.
Beneath white yams' brown skin is an appetizing, starchy, fibrous white flesh, which has an earthy, largely neutral, flavour, tinged with a very faint sweetness - the flavour is comparable to that of potatoes. Indeed, in the regions they hail from they are in a similar fashion to how we consume potatoes in the UK, and have thus long been a staple food in Asian, African, and Caribbean cuisine. Their mild taste means they are excellent at soaking up the flavour of spices.
It is their nutritional benefits, however, that really entice people to eat white yams. Not only are they an excellent source of dietary fibre, but they are also rich in various minerals, including potassium and magnesium, several antioxidants, and have a high content of a unique, naturally-occurring compound called 'diosgenin', which is believed to boost intellectual functions such as memory.
As aforementioned, white yams are usually consumed like potatoes, so boiling, frying and roasting are the most common ways of cooking them. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for recipes on how to make a delicious white yam stew and some traditional 'pounded yam' to accompany it?
